vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.title: Classifications of Data Structures (Primitive & Non-Primitive)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.simpleConcept: Think of data structures like kitchen containers. A single spice jar holds one item (primitive data types like int, float, char). A layered bento box or spice rack organizes multiple items together in a structured way (non-primitive data structures like arrays, stacks, and linked lists). Choosing the right container makes cooking (computing) fast and clean.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.technicalConcept:
Data structures are categorized into:
1. Primitive Data Structures: Basic types directly supported by hardware and machine instructions (int, float, char, pointer, double).
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures: Derived complex structures organizing collections of data elements.
   • Linear Data Structures: Elements form a sequential sequence (Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists). In linear structures, elements have unique predecessors and successors (except first and last).
   • Non-Linear Data Structures: Elements form hierarchical or interconnected relationships (Trees, Graphs). Each element may connect to multiple items.
keyPoints: Primitive types (int, char, float) operate directly via CPU registers and ALU instructions.
Non-primitive types organize multiple homogeneous or heterogeneous values.
Linear data structures maintain single-level sequential relationships (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues).
Non-linear structures represent hierarchical (Trees) or arbitrary network relationships (Graphs).
Primary operations include Insertion, Deletion, Traversal, Searching, Sorting, and Merging.

examModelAnswers.question: Define data structure. Explain the classification of data structures with a neat block diagram.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
A data structure is a specialized format for organizing, processing, retrieving, and storing data in computer memory efficiently.

2. Classification Hierarchy:
• Primitive Data Structures: Native machine types (int, float, char, pointer).
• Non-Primitive Data Structures:
  a) Linear Data Structures: Single-level sequence where elements are adjacent.
     - Arrays: Fixed-size contiguous memory blocks.
     - Stacks: LIFO (Last In First Out) collections.
     - Queues: FIFO (First In First Out) collections.
     - Linked Lists: Nodes dynamically linked via memory pointers.
  b) Non-Linear Data Structures: Multi-level non-sequential collections.
     - Trees: Hierarchical parent-child relationship (Binary Tree, BST, AVL).
     - Graphs: Many-to-many relationship of vertices and edges.

3. Core Operations:
Traverse, Insert, Delete, Search, Sort, Merge.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory Allocation in C
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.simpleConcept: A pointer is a note with a house address instead of the house itself. Dynamic memory allocation is like booking a hotel room: you don't decide how many rooms you need when building the hotel (compile-time); you ask the front desk (OS) for exactly the rooms you need when guests arrive (runtime using malloc/calloc), and you must check out (free) when you leave so memory isn't wasted.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.technicalConcept:
Pointers store memory addresses of variables. The dereference operator `*` accesses the value at that address, while address-of `&` retrieves the memory address.
Dynamic Memory Allocation (DMA) allocates heap memory at runtime via standard library `<stdlib.h>` functions:
1. `malloc(size)`: Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes; returns `void*` or NULL on failure.
2. `calloc(n, size)`: Allocates contiguous block for `n` items of `size` bytes each and initializes all bits to 0.
3. `realloc(ptr, new_size)`: Resizes previously allocated heap block, preserving existing content.
4. `free(ptr)`: Deallocates heap block to prevent memory leaks.
keyPoints: Pointer declaration `type *ptr` holds an address in virtual memory.
malloc() leaves allocated memory uninitialized with garbage values.
calloc() clears memory to zero, useful for arrays and counters.
Always check `ptr != NULL` after heap allocations to avoid segmentation faults.
Failing to call `free()` leads to memory leaks; accessing after `free()` creates dangling pointer bugs.

examModelAnswers.question: Differentiate between malloc() and calloc(). Explain dynamic memory allocation with a complete C code example.

1. Difference Table:
• Parameter: `malloc(size_t size)` takes total bytes; `calloc(size_t n, size_t size)` takes count and unit size.
• Initialization: `malloc` leaves memory uninitialized (garbage); `calloc` initializes all allocated bytes to zero.
• Performance: `malloc` is slightly faster as it skips zeroing memory.

2. Realloc and Free:
• `realloc(ptr, new_size)` dynamically expands or contracts existing memory block.
• `free(ptr)` returns memory back to heap pool.

3. Syntax and Check:
```c
int *p = (int*)malloc(n * sizeof(int));
if (p == NULL) { /* Handle OOM */ }
free(p);
p = NULL;
```

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.title: Arrays & Dynamic Allocation Arrays
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.simpleConcept: A static array is like a locked bookshelf with 5 fixed slots built into the wall. If you buy a 6th book, you are stuck. A dynamic array is a modular shelf on wheels: you can allocate 5 slots today, and if you need more space, you order a bigger shelf, move your books over, and discard the old one.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.technicalConcept:
Arrays are contiguous blocks of homogeneous data elements accessible via zero-based indexing.
• 1D Array Address Formula: `Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + (i - LowerBound) * ElementSize`
• 2D Row-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(i * ColCount) + j] * ElementSize`
• 2D Column-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(j * RowCount) + i] * ElementSize`
Dynamic arrays overcome fixed compile-time dimensions by allocating heap pointers through `malloc/realloc`.
keyPoints: Arrays guarantee O(1) constant time random access by index.
Insertion and deletion in arbitrary positions require O(n) element shifting.
Row-major order stores elements row-by-row in linear memory (standard in C/C++).
Dynamic 2D arrays can be created via an array of pointers (`int **mat = malloc(rows * sizeof(int*))`).

examModelAnswers.question: Derive the address formula for a 2-dimensional array stored in Row-Major and Column-Major order.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
Let array A have bounds A[0...M-1][0...N-1], Base address = B, and element size = w bytes.

1. Row-Major Order:
• Elements are stored row-by-row.
• To reach element A[i][j], we must skip 'i' complete rows. Each row has 'N' elements, so `i * N` elements precede the current row.
• In row 'i', we must skip 'j' elements to reach column 'j'.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(i * N) + j] * w`.

2. Column-Major Order:
• Elements are stored column-by-column.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(j * M) + i] * w`.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.title: Structures, Unions & Polynomial Representation
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.simpleConcept: A structure is like a wallet that holds your ID card, money, and keys at the same time—each item gets its own space. A union is like a single phone pocket that can hold either your credit card OR your transit pass, but not both at once. For polynomials like 5x² + 3x + 1, structures allow us to bundle coefficient and exponent pairs neatly.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.technicalConcept:
• `struct`: Composite data type where every member has its own distinct memory offset. Total size >= sum of member sizes (plus padding).
• `union`: Members share the exact same starting memory address. Total size = size of its largest member.
• Polynomial Representation: A polynomial P(x) = a_n x^e + ... + a_0 is represented in memory as an array of structures or linked list where each node stores `coefficient` and `exponent`.
keyPoints: Struct members coexist simultaneously; union members share the same memory location.
Arrow operator `ptr->member` dereferences and accesses struct members through pointers.
Polynomial addition compares exponents: if equal, add coefficients; if unequal, copy higher exponent term.
Unions save memory when only one of multiple mutual fields is valid at any time.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.title: Sparse Matrix Representation (Triplet Form)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.simpleConcept: Imagine an attendance sheet with 1,000 students where only 3 students are absent. Instead of printing 1,000 names with 'Present' next to 997 of them, you just write down the 3 roll numbers who are absent. That is a sparse matrix: when most entries are zeros, we only store the non-zero values with their (row, column, value) coordinates.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.technicalConcept:
A sparse matrix is an M x N matrix in which the majority of elements are zero. Storing all elements in a standard 2D array wastes memory (O(M x N)) and CPU cycles processing zeroes.
Triplet Representation (3-Tuple Form):
An array of structures where each element has:
• `row`: Row index of non-zero value
• `col`: Column index of non-zero value
• `val`: Non-zero value
Row 0 (Header/Metadata) stores:
• `triplet[0].row = Total Rows (M)`
• `triplet[0].col = Total Columns (N)`
• `triplet[0].val = Total Non-Zero Elements (K)`
The total space occupied is (K + 1) * 3, dramatically smaller when K << M * N.
keyPoints: A matrix is sparse if zero elements significantly outnumber non-zero elements.
Standard 2D array uses O(rows * cols); Triplet form uses O(non_zeros) storage.
Row 0 is the metadata header storing matrix dimensions and total non-zero count.
Triplets are traditionally sorted by row index, then by column index.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.title: Transposing a Sparse Matrix
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.simpleConcept: Transposing means turning rows into columns (swapping i and j coordinates). If you just swap coordinates naively, the resulting triplet list won't be sorted by rows anymore! An ordinary transpose searches through all columns one by one, which is slow. Fast Transpose uses a frequency count to precalculate the exact destination slot for every element in one smooth pass.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.technicalConcept:
When transposing a sparse triplet representation, swapping `row` and `col` invalidates row-major ordering.
1. Ordinary Transpose: Iterates columns 0 to N-1; scans all K non-zero elements. Time: O(Cols * K).
2. Fast Transpose: Uses `row_terms[]` and `starting_pos[]` to place elements directly into target slots in a single pass. Time: O(Cols + K).
keyPoints: Transposing swaps (row, col) coordinates while preserving sorted row order.
Ordinary Transpose has O(cols * non_zeros) time complexity.
Fast Transpose achieves O(cols + non_zeros) using row_terms[] and starting_pos[] auxiliary arrays.
Fast Transpose requires O(cols) auxiliary memory space.

examModelAnswers.question: Write and explain the Fast Transpose algorithm for sparse matrix representation. Analyze its time complexity.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Concept & Need:
In ordinary transpose, scanning all terms for every column costs O(cols * terms). Fast Transpose uses two auxiliary arrays to achieve O(cols + terms).

2. Auxiliary Arrays:
• `row_terms[col]`: Frequency count of elements in column `col` of matrix A.
• `starting_pos[col]`: Prefix sum starting index in transposed matrix B: `starting_pos[i] = starting_pos[i-1] + row_terms[i-1]` with `starting_pos[0] = 1`.

3. Complexity Analysis:
• Loop 1: O(terms)
• Loop 2: O(cols)
• Loop 3: O(terms)
Total Time Complexity = O(cols + terms), which is linear.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.title: Stack Definition, Array Representation & Operations
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.simpleConcept: A stack is like a spring-loaded plate dispenser in a cafeteria: plates can only be added to or removed from the very top (LIFO: Last In, First Out). The last clean plate placed on top is the first one taken by the next customer.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.technicalConcept:
A Stack is a restricted linear data structure operating under the LIFO (Last-In First-Out) discipline where all insertions and deletions occur at a single end called `top`.
• Array Representation: An array `stack[MAX]` with integer pointer `top` initialized to `-1`.
• Push Operation: Check overflow (`top == MAX - 1`), increment `top`, and store `stack[++top] = item` (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
• Pop Operation: Check underflow (`top == -1`), retrieve `item = stack[top--]` (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
• Peek Operation: Inspect element at `top` without modifying pointer state (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
keyPoints: Stack enforces strict LIFO (Last-In First-Out) access control.
Stack Overflow occurs when attempting push on full array (top == MAX - 1).
Stack Underflow occurs when attempting pop on empty array (top == -1).
All core operations (push, pop, peek, isEmpty, isFull) execute in O(1) constant time.
Common applications: Function call runtime stack, recursive backtracking, syntax parsing, and undo-redo buffers.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.title: Stacks using Dynamic Arrays
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.simpleConcept: A static stack is like a fixed-size egg carton with 6 slots; once full, you can't add more. A dynamic stack is like an accordion file that automatically doubles in size whenever you run out of slots, copying your files over smoothly.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.technicalConcept:
Fixed-size array stacks suffer from static memory limits. Dynamic array stacks allocate memory on the heap and automatically double capacity when full.
• Allocation: Initially allocate `capacity` elements via `malloc()`.
• Doubling Strategy: When `top == capacity - 1`, allocate `newCapacity = 2 * capacity` via `realloc()`.
• Amortized Complexity: While an occasional reallocation costs $O(N)$ copying time, the amortized cost per push over $N$ insertions remains $O(1)$.
• Memory Cleanup: Requires `free()` on stack destruction to prevent heap memory leaks.
keyPoints: Overcomes fixed compile-time stack limits using heap dynamic memory.
Uses realloc() to resize the contiguous memory block.
Doubling strategy achieves O(1) amortized push complexity.
Always verify realloc return pointer != NULL before overwriting existing pointer.
Must free the allocated buffer when stack lifecycle terminates.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.title: Polish Notation (Infix, Prefix, Postfix)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.simpleConcept: When humans write math, we place operators between numbers (Infix: A + B). But computers find parentheses and operator precedence messy. Polish notation puts operators in front (Prefix: + A B) or after (Postfix: A B +), removing all need for parentheses.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.technicalConcept:
Notations for arithmetic expressions:
1. Infix Notation: Operator is placed between operands: `A + B`. Requires operator precedence, associativity, and parentheses for unambiguous evaluation.
2. Prefix (Polish) Notation: Operator precedes operands: `+ A B`.
3. Postfix (Reverse Polish) Notation: Operator follows operands: `A B +`.
• Operator Precedence Hierarchy: Parentheses `()` > Exponentiation `^` ($R \to L$) > Multiplication/Division `*`, `/` ($L \to R$) > Addition/Subtraction `+`, `-` ($L \to R$).
• Advantages of Postfix: Eliminates parentheses, does not require look-ahead parsing, and evaluates linearly using a single stack pass.
keyPoints: Infix requires operator precedence, associativity, and parentheses rules.
Postfix and Prefix require NO parentheses and NO precedence parsing during evaluation.
Exponentiation (^) is Right-to-Left associative; +, -, *, / are Left-to-Right associative.
Computers and compilers convert source infix expressions to postfix bytecode.
Postfix expressions are parsed in a single linear O(N) scan using an operand stack.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.title: Circular Queues (Array & Dynamic)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.simpleConcept: A circular queue is like a revolving sushi bar or carousel: when you reach the last seat at the end of the counter, the next seat wraps right back around to seat 0, ensuring no empty space is ever wasted.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.technicalConcept:
Circular Queues eliminate the false overflow of linear queues by conceptually connecting `MAX - 1` back to `0` using modulo arithmetic.
• Pointer Increment: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX` and `front = (front + 1) % MAX`.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front` (reserves one sentinel slot to distinguish full from empty).
• Empty Condition: `front == rear`.
• Dynamic Circular Queue: When full, reallocates array with double capacity and unwraps the circular segments `[front...MAX-1]` and `[0...rear]` into a clean linear contiguous sequence `0...N-1`.
keyPoints: Uses modulo arithmetic (rear + 1) % MAX to wrap pointers around array boundaries.

examModelAnswers.question: What is a circular queue? Write C functions for insert and delete in circular queue and explain how it solves linear queue false overflow.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
A Circular Queue is a linear data structure where the last position connects back to the first position, forming a ring buffer.

2. Modulo Arithmetic:
`rear = (rear + 1) % MAX` and `front = (front + 1) % MAX`.

3. Solution to False Overflow:
In linear queues, when `rear == MAX - 1`, new elements cannot enter even if `front > 0`. Circular queues wrap `rear` back to index 0, utilizing freed front slots.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.title: Multiple Stacks and Queues
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: Multiple stacks in one array is like sharing a long double-ended train car: Stack 1 starts filling seats from the front moving backward, while Stack 2 starts filling seats from the back moving forward. They only collide when the entire train is completely full.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
Partitioning a single contiguous array `V[MAX]` to house multiple stacks or queues:
1. Two Stacks in One Array: `top1` starts at `-1` growing rightward (`++top1`), `top2` starts at `MAX` growing leftward (`--top2`). Overflow occurs only when `top1 + 1 == top2`, achieving optimal space sharing.
2. N Stacks in One Array: Divide array into $N$ equal segments of size `MAX / N` with boundary pointers `B[i]` and top pointers `T[i]`. If stack $i$ exceeds its segment, shift boundary pointers or reallocate dynamically.
3. Multiple Queues: Similarly divide array into $N$ segments with separate `front[i]` and `rear[i]` pointers.
keyPoints: Two stacks growing towards each other utilize 100% of memory before overflowing.
Overflow for 2 stacks occurs only when top1 + 1 == top2.
N stacks in one array divide memory into segments with boundary B[i] and top T[i].
Dynamic boundary shifting allows an overflowing stack to borrow space from an adjacent underutilized stack.
Conserves memory overhead compared to allocating separate fixed-size buffers.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.title: Tree Terminology & Binary Trees Properties
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.simpleConcept: A tree data structure is like an inverted family pedigree or organizational chart: the CEO (root) sits at the very top, managers branch out below (internal nodes), and team members without direct reports are at the bottom (leaves).
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.technicalConcept:
A Tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of one root node and zero or more disjoint subtrees.
• Terminology:
  - Root: Unique top node with in-degree 0.
  - Degree of node: Number of subtrees/children attached to the node.
  - Leaf/Terminal node: Node with degree 0.
  - Level: Root is at level 0; children are at level + 1.
  - Height/Depth: Maximum level of any node in the tree.
• Binary Tree: Tree where every node has at most 2 children (left child and right child).
• Core Mathematical Properties:
  1. Maximum nodes at level $i$: $2^i$.
  2. Maximum nodes in binary tree of height $k$: $2^{k+1} - 1$.
  3. Leaf Node Formula: For any non-empty binary tree, $n_0 = n_2 + 1$ (leaves equals degree-2 nodes plus 1).
keyPoints: Trees represent hierarchical parent-child relationships.
Binary tree restricts each node to at most two children (left and right).
Maximum nodes at level i is 2^i (assuming root at level 0).
Maximum nodes in binary tree of depth k is 2^(k+1) - 1.
Fundamental relation: Number of leaf nodes n0 is always n2 + 1 (nodes of degree 2 plus 1).

examModelAnswers.question: Define the following tree terms: Root, Degree, Depth, Leaf, Path. Prove that for any non-empty binary tree with n nodes and e edges, e = n - 1.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:

• Degree: Number of direct children of a node.
• Leaf: Node with degree 0.
• Depth: Length of path from root to node.
• Path: Sequence of consecutive edges connecting nodes.

2. Proof of e = n - 1:
Every node in a tree except the root has exactly one incoming edge from its parent. Since there are n nodes and only the root has no parent, the total number of incoming edges must be n - 1. Thus, e = n - 1.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.title: Array and Linked Representation of Binary Trees
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.simpleConcept: Storing a binary tree in an array is like assigning house numbers on a planned street: parent house i always has left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2. Linked representation is like freeform land where each house has two directional pointers pointing to neighbor lots.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.technicalConcept:
Two fundamental ways to represent binary trees in memory:
1. Sequential (Array) Representation:
• Store nodes in a 1D array `tree[MAX]` using level-order index mapping (0-based):
  - Left child of node `i`: `2 * i + 1`
  - Right child of node `i`: `2 * i + 2`
  - Parent of node `i`: `(i - 1) / 2`
• Pros: Direct random access without pointers.
• Cons: Wastes massive space ($O(2^h)$) for skewed binary trees.
2. Linked (Pointer) Representation:
• Each node has `data`, `left` pointer, and `right` pointer (`struct TreeNode*`).
• Pros: Efficient memory allocation scaling directly with $N$ nodes ($O(N)$ space).
• Cons: Extra pointer memory overhead.
keyPoints: Array representation maps node i to left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2.
Array representation is optimal for Complete Binary Trees (compact storage).
Array representation wastes significant space for sparse or skewed trees.
Linked representation uses left and right pointers per node, dynamically allocated.
Linked representation is the universal standard for non-complete trees.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.title: Graph ADT & Elementary Graph Operations
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.simpleConcept: A graph is like a city airline route map: airports are vertices (nodes) and direct flights are edges. Breadth-First Search spreads like a radar wave (layer-by-layer), while Depth-First Search explores one flight connection to the end of the line before backtracking.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.technicalConcept:
A Graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of vertices $V$ and edges $E$.
1. Representations:
• Adjacency Matrix: $V \times V$ 2D array where `adj[u][v] = 1` if edge $(u,v)$ exists ($O(V^2)$ space).
• Adjacency List: Array of $V$ linked lists where `list[u]` stores all neighbors of $u$ ($O(V + E)$ space, optimal for sparse graphs).
2. Elementary Operations:
• Breadth-First Search (BFS): Explores vertices level-by-level using an auxiliary FIFO Queue ($O(V + E)$).
• Depth-First Search (DFS): Explores as deep as possible along each branch using recursion / Stack ($O(V + E)$).
• Connected Components: Finding maximal connected subgraphs using DFS/BFS sweeps.
keyPoints: Adjacency Matrix uses O(V^2) space; ideal for dense graphs.
Adjacency List uses O(V + E) space; optimal for sparse graphs.
BFS uses a FIFO queue and finds shortest unweighted paths.
DFS uses a stack or recursion and is used for cycle detection and topological sorting.
Both BFS and DFS maintain a visited[] boolean array to avoid infinite loops in cyclic graphs.

vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.title: Hashing (Introduction & Static Hashing)
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.simpleConcept: Hashing is like coat-check at a theater: instead of searching every coat on the rack (O(N)), the attendant hands you ticket number 42 derived directly from your token, so you walk straight to hook 42 in O(1) instant time.
vtu-ise-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.technicalConcept:
Hashing maps a large key space to a compact array index `0...m-1` (Hash Table) using a Hash Function $h(k)$.
1. Common Hash Functions:
• Division Method: $h(k) = k \pmod{m}$ ($m$ prime close to table size).
• Mid-Square Method: Square key $k^2$ and extract middle $r$ digits.
• Folding Method: Divide key into parts and sum them.
2. Collision Resolution Techniques (Open Addressing & Chaining):
• Collision: When $h(k_1) = h(k_2)$ for $k_1 \neq k_2$.
• Linear Probing: When collision occurs, probe consecutive slots `(h(k) + i) % m`. Suffers from Primary Clustering.
• Quadratic Probing: Probes `(h(k) + i^2) % m`. Reduces clustering.
• Separate Chaining: Each slot points to a linked list of collided keys ($O(1 + \alpha)$ average access where $\alpha = n/m$ is load factor).
keyPoints: Hash function maps large arbitrary keys to compact table index in O(1) time.
Collision occurs when two distinct keys hash to the same table index.
Linear Probing resolves collisions by checking next consecutive slot (suffers from clustering).
Quadratic Probing uses (h(k) + i^2) % m to eliminate primary clustering.
Separate Chaining stores collisions in an external linked list at each table bucket.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.title: Classifications of Data Structures (Primitive & Non-Primitive)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.simpleConcept: Think of data structures like kitchen containers. A single spice jar holds one item (primitive data types like int, float, char). A layered bento box or spice rack organizes multiple items together in a structured way (non-primitive data structures like arrays, stacks, and linked lists). Choosing the right container makes cooking (computing) fast and clean.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t1.technicalConcept:
Data structures are categorized into:
1. Primitive Data Structures: Basic types directly supported by hardware and machine instructions (int, float, char, pointer, double).
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures: Derived complex structures organizing collections of data elements.
   • Linear Data Structures: Elements form a sequential sequence (Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists). In linear structures, elements have unique predecessors and successors (except first and last).
   • Non-Linear Data Structures: Elements form hierarchical or interconnected relationships (Trees, Graphs). Each element may connect to multiple items.
keyPoints: Primitive types (int, char, float) operate directly via CPU registers and ALU instructions.
Non-primitive types organize multiple homogeneous or heterogeneous values.
Linear data structures maintain single-level sequential relationships (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues).
Non-linear structures represent hierarchical (Trees) or arbitrary network relationships (Graphs).
Primary operations include Insertion, Deletion, Traversal, Searching, Sorting, and Merging.

     - Stacks: LIFO (Last In First Out) collections.

  b) Non-Linear Data Structures: Multi-level non-sequential collections.
     - Trees: Hierarchical parent-child relationship (Binary Tree, BST, AVL).
     - Graphs: Many-to-many relationship of vertices and edges.

3. Core Operations:
Traverse, Insert, Delete, Search, Sort, Merge.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory Allocation in C
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.simpleConcept: A pointer is a note with a house address instead of the house itself. Dynamic memory allocation is like booking a hotel room: you don't decide how many rooms you need when building the hotel (compile-time); you ask the front desk (OS) for exactly the rooms you need when guests arrive (runtime using malloc/calloc), and you must check out (free) when you leave so memory isn't wasted.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t2.technicalConcept:
Pointers store memory addresses of variables. The dereference operator `*` accesses the value at that address, while address-of `&` retrieves the memory address.
Dynamic Memory Allocation (DMA) allocates heap memory at runtime via standard library `<stdlib.h>` functions:
1. `malloc(size)`: Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes; returns `void*` or NULL on failure.
2. `calloc(n, size)`: Allocates contiguous block for `n` items of `size` bytes each and initializes all bits to 0.
3. `realloc(ptr, new_size)`: Resizes previously allocated heap block, preserving existing content.
4. `free(ptr)`: Deallocates heap block to prevent memory leaks.
keyPoints: Pointer declaration `type *ptr` holds an address in virtual memory.
malloc() leaves allocated memory uninitialized with garbage values.
calloc() clears memory to zero, useful for arrays and counters.
Always check `ptr != NULL` after heap allocations to avoid segmentation faults.
Failing to call `free()` leads to memory leaks; accessing after `free()` creates dangling pointer bugs.

examModelAnswers.question: Differentiate between malloc() and calloc(). Explain dynamic memory allocation with a complete C code example.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Difference Table:
• Parameter: `malloc(size_t size)` takes total bytes; `calloc(size_t n, size_t size)` takes count and unit size.
• Initialization: `malloc` leaves memory uninitialized (garbage); `calloc` initializes all allocated bytes to zero.
• Performance: `malloc` is slightly faster as it skips zeroing memory.

2. Realloc and Free:
• `realloc(ptr, new_size)` dynamically expands or contracts existing memory block.
• `free(ptr)` returns memory back to heap pool.

3. Syntax and Check:
```c
int *p = (int*)malloc(n * sizeof(int));
if (p == NULL) { /* Handle OOM */ }
free(p);
p = NULL;
```

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.title: Arrays & Dynamic Allocation Arrays
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.simpleConcept: A static array is like a locked bookshelf with 5 fixed slots built into the wall. If you buy a 6th book, you are stuck. A dynamic array is a modular shelf on wheels: you can allocate 5 slots today, and if you need more space, you order a bigger shelf, move your books over, and discard the old one.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t3.technicalConcept:
Arrays are contiguous blocks of homogeneous data elements accessible via zero-based indexing.
• 1D Array Address Formula: `Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + (i - LowerBound) * ElementSize`
• 2D Row-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(i * ColCount) + j] * ElementSize`
• 2D Column-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(j * RowCount) + i] * ElementSize`
Dynamic arrays overcome fixed compile-time dimensions by allocating heap pointers through `malloc/realloc`.
keyPoints: Arrays guarantee O(1) constant time random access by index.
Insertion and deletion in arbitrary positions require O(n) element shifting.
Row-major order stores elements row-by-row in linear memory (standard in C/C++).
Dynamic 2D arrays can be created via an array of pointers (`int **mat = malloc(rows * sizeof(int*))`).

examModelAnswers.question: Derive the address formula for a 2-dimensional array stored in Row-Major and Column-Major order.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
Let array A have bounds A[0...M-1][0...N-1], Base address = B, and element size = w bytes.

1. Row-Major Order:
• Elements are stored row-by-row.
• To reach element A[i][j], we must skip 'i' complete rows. Each row has 'N' elements, so `i * N` elements precede the current row.
• In row 'i', we must skip 'j' elements to reach column 'j'.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(i * N) + j] * w`.

2. Column-Major Order:
• Elements are stored column-by-column.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(j * M) + i] * w`.
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Award 3.5 marks for Row-Major derivation, and 3.5 marks for Column-Major derivation.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.title: Structures, Unions & Polynomial Representation
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.simpleConcept: A structure is like a wallet that holds your ID card, money, and keys at the same time—each item gets its own space. A union is like a single phone pocket that can hold either your credit card OR your transit pass, but not both at once. For polynomials like 5x² + 3x + 1, structures allow us to bundle coefficient and exponent pairs neatly.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t4.technicalConcept:
• `struct`: Composite data type where every member has its own distinct memory offset. Total size >= sum of member sizes (plus padding).
• `union`: Members share the exact same starting memory address. Total size = size of its largest member.
• Polynomial Representation: A polynomial P(x) = a_n x^e + ... + a_0 is represented in memory as an array of structures or linked list where each node stores `coefficient` and `exponent`.
keyPoints: Struct members coexist simultaneously; union members share the same memory location.
Arrow operator `ptr->member` dereferences and accesses struct members through pointers.
Polynomial addition compares exponents: if equal, add coefficients; if unequal, copy higher exponent term.
Unions save memory when only one of multiple mutual fields is valid at any time.

examModelAnswers.question: Differentiate between structures and unions in C. Explain polynomial representation using an array of structures.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Structure vs Union Comparison:
• Memory: `struct` allocates separate memory for each member; `union` shares memory equal to the largest member.
• Access: In `struct`, all members can be accessed at the same time; in `union`, only one member can be reliably accessed at any given moment.
• Keyword: `struct` vs `union`.

2. Polynomial Representation:
```c
struct Term { float coeff; int exp; };
struct Term poly[MAX_TERMS];
```
• Terms are arranged in descending order of exponents.
• During addition, compare exponents: if equal, add coefficients; if unequal, attach the higher degree term directly.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.simpleConcept: Imagine an attendance sheet with 1,000 students where only 3 students are absent. Instead of printing 1,000 names with 'Present' next to 997 of them, you just write down the 3 roll numbers who are absent. That is a sparse matrix: when most entries are zeros, we only store the non-zero values with their (row, column, value) coordinates.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t5.technicalConcept:
A sparse matrix is an M x N matrix in which the majority of elements are zero. Storing all elements in a standard 2D array wastes memory (O(M x N)) and CPU cycles processing zeroes.
Triplet Representation (3-Tuple Form):
An array of structures where each element has:
• `row`: Row index of non-zero value
• `col`: Column index of non-zero value
• `val`: Non-zero value
Row 0 (Header/Metadata) stores:
• `triplet[0].row = Total Rows (M)`
• `triplet[0].col = Total Columns (N)`
• `triplet[0].val = Total Non-Zero Elements (K)`
The total space occupied is (K + 1) * 3, dramatically smaller when K << M * N.
keyPoints: A matrix is sparse if zero elements significantly outnumber non-zero elements.
Standard 2D array uses O(rows * cols); Triplet form uses O(non_zeros) storage.
Row 0 is the metadata header storing matrix dimensions and total non-zero count.
Triplets are traditionally sorted by row index, then by column index.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.title: Transposing a Sparse Matrix
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.simpleConcept: Transposing means turning rows into columns (swapping i and j coordinates). If you just swap coordinates naively, the resulting triplet list won't be sorted by rows anymore! An ordinary transpose searches through all columns one by one, which is slow. Fast Transpose uses a frequency count to precalculate the exact destination slot for every element in one smooth pass.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m1-t6.technicalConcept:
When transposing a sparse triplet representation, swapping `row` and `col` invalidates row-major ordering.
1. Ordinary Transpose: Iterates columns 0 to N-1; scans all K non-zero elements. Time: O(Cols * K).
2. Fast Transpose: Uses `row_terms[]` and `starting_pos[]` to place elements directly into target slots in a single pass. Time: O(Cols + K).
keyPoints: Transposing swaps (row, col) coordinates while preserving sorted row order.
Ordinary Transpose has O(cols * non_zeros) time complexity.
Fast Transpose achieves O(cols + non_zeros) using row_terms[] and starting_pos[] auxiliary arrays.
Fast Transpose requires O(cols) auxiliary memory space.

examModelAnswers.question: Write and explain the Fast Transpose algorithm for sparse matrix representation. Analyze its time complexity.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Concept & Need:
In ordinary transpose, scanning all terms for every column costs O(cols * terms). Fast Transpose uses two auxiliary arrays to achieve O(cols + terms).

2. Auxiliary Arrays:
• `row_terms[col]`: Frequency count of elements in column `col` of matrix A.
• `starting_pos[col]`: Prefix sum starting index in transposed matrix B: `starting_pos[i] = starting_pos[i-1] + row_terms[i-1]` with `starting_pos[0] = 1`.

3. Complexity Analysis:
• Loop 1: O(terms)
• Loop 2: O(cols)
• Loop 3: O(terms)
Total Time Complexity = O(cols + terms), which is linear.
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Award 2 marks for algorithm logic, 3 marks for C code/pseudocode, 2 marks for array explanations, and 1 mark for complexity analysis.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.title: Stack Definition, Array Representation & Operations
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.simpleConcept: A stack is like a spring-loaded plate dispenser in a cafeteria: plates can only be added to or removed from the very top (LIFO: Last In, First Out). The last clean plate placed on top is the first one taken by the next customer.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t1.technicalConcept:
A Stack is a restricted linear data structure operating under the LIFO (Last-In First-Out) discipline where all insertions and deletions occur at a single end called `top`.
• Array Representation: An array `stack[MAX]` with integer pointer `top` initialized to `-1`.
• Push Operation: Check overflow (`top == MAX - 1`), increment `top`, and store `stack[++top] = item` (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
• Pop Operation: Check underflow (`top == -1`), retrieve `item = stack[top--]` (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
• Peek Operation: Inspect element at `top` without modifying pointer state (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
keyPoints: Stack enforces strict LIFO (Last-In First-Out) access control.
Stack Overflow occurs when attempting push on full array (top == MAX - 1).
Stack Underflow occurs when attempting pop on empty array (top == -1).
All core operations (push, pop, peek, isEmpty, isFull) execute in O(1) constant time.
Common applications: Function call runtime stack, recursive backtracking, syntax parsing, and undo-redo buffers.

examModelAnswers.question: Define a stack. Explain the primitive operations performed on a stack with C functions and appropriate status checks.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
A Stack is an ordered collection of homogeneous items in which insertion and deletion occur exclusively at one end called the `top` (LIFO).

2. Primitive Operations:
• Push(x): Inserts element x at top. Pre-condition: top < MAX - 1.
• Pop(): Deletes and returns top element. Pre-condition: top >= 0.
• Peek(): Returns top element without deletion.
• Display(): Traverses from top down to 0.

3. Overflow & Underflow Conditions:
• Overflow: `top == MAX - 1`
• Underflow: `top == -1`.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.title: Stacks using Dynamic Arrays
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.simpleConcept: A static stack is like a fixed-size egg carton with 6 slots; once full, you can't add more. A dynamic stack is like an accordion file that automatically doubles in size whenever you run out of slots, copying your files over smoothly.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t2.technicalConcept:
Fixed-size array stacks suffer from static memory limits. Dynamic array stacks allocate memory on the heap and automatically double capacity when full.
• Allocation: Initially allocate `capacity` elements via `malloc()`.
• Doubling Strategy: When `top == capacity - 1`, allocate `newCapacity = 2 * capacity` via `realloc()`.
• Amortized Complexity: While an occasional reallocation costs $O(N)$ copying time, the amortized cost per push over $N$ insertions remains $O(1)$.
• Memory Cleanup: Requires `free()` on stack destruction to prevent heap memory leaks.
keyPoints: Overcomes fixed compile-time stack limits using heap dynamic memory.
Uses realloc() to resize the contiguous memory block.
Doubling strategy achieves O(1) amortized push complexity.

1BCS305_M2_T2.simpleConcept: A static stack is like a fixed-size egg carton with 6 slots; once full, you can't add more. A dynamic stack is like an accordion file that automatically doubles in size whenever you run out of slots, copying your files over smoothly.

Fixed-size array stacks suffer from static memory limits. Dynamic array stacks allocate memory on the heap and automatically double capacity when full.
• Allocation: Initially allocate `capacity` elements via `malloc()`.

• Memory Cleanup: Requires `free()` on stack destruction to prevent heap memory leaks.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.title: Polish Notation (Infix, Prefix, Postfix)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.simpleConcept: When humans write math, we place operators between numbers (Infix: A + B). But computers find parentheses and operator precedence messy. Polish notation puts operators in front (Prefix: + A B) or after (Postfix: A B +), removing all need for parentheses.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t3.technicalConcept:
Notations for arithmetic expressions:
1. Infix Notation: Operator is placed between operands: `A + B`. Requires operator precedence, associativity, and parentheses for unambiguous evaluation.
2. Prefix (Polish) Notation: Operator precedes operands: `+ A B`.
3. Postfix (Reverse Polish) Notation: Operator follows operands: `A B +`.
• Operator Precedence Hierarchy: Parentheses `()` > Exponentiation `^` ($R \to L$) > Multiplication/Division `*`, `/` ($L \to R$) > Addition/Subtraction `+`, `-` ($L \to R$).
• Advantages of Postfix: Eliminates parentheses, does not require look-ahead parsing, and evaluates linearly using a single stack pass.
keyPoints: Infix requires operator precedence, associativity, and parentheses rules.
Postfix and Prefix require NO parentheses and NO precedence parsing during evaluation.
Exponentiation (^) is Right-to-Left associative; +, -, *, / are Left-to-Right associative.
Computers and compilers convert source infix expressions to postfix bytecode.
Postfix expressions are parsed in a single linear O(N) scan using an operand stack.

1. Definition:
Polish notation (devised by Jan Łukasiewicz) is a notation format where operator placement determines evaluation order without parentheses.

• Infix: `<operand> <operator> <operand>` (e.g. `(A + B) * C`)
• Prefix: `<operator> <operand> <operand>` (e.g. `* + A B C`)
• Postfix: `<operand> <operand> <operator>` (e.g. `A B + C *`)

3. Advantages:
Postfix expressions can be evaluated directly in one forward scan using a stack.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.title: Circular Queues (Array & Dynamic)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.simpleConcept: A circular queue is like a revolving sushi bar or carousel: when you reach the last seat at the end of the counter, the next seat wraps right back around to seat 0, ensuring no empty space is ever wasted.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t1.technicalConcept:
Circular Queues eliminate the false overflow of linear queues by conceptually connecting `MAX - 1` back to `0` using modulo arithmetic.
• Pointer Increment: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX` and `front = (front + 1) % MAX`.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front` (reserves one sentinel slot to distinguish full from empty).
• Empty Condition: `front == rear`.
• Dynamic Circular Queue: When full, reallocates array with double capacity and unwraps the circular segments `[front...MAX-1]` and `[0...rear]` into a clean linear contiguous sequence `0...N-1`.
keyPoints: Uses modulo arithmetic (rear + 1) % MAX to wrap pointers around array boundaries.
Eliminates false overflow and achieves 100% space utilization.
Empty condition: front == rear. Full condition: (rear + 1) % MAX == front.
One array slot is reserved as a sentinel to distinguish full from empty states.
Dynamic circular queue requires linear unwrapping during realloc buffer expansion.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.title: Multiple Stacks and Queues
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: Multiple stacks in one array is like sharing a long double-ended train car: Stack 1 starts filling seats from the front moving backward, while Stack 2 starts filling seats from the back moving forward. They only collide when the entire train is completely full.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
Partitioning a single contiguous array `V[MAX]` to house multiple stacks or queues:
1. Two Stacks in One Array: `top1` starts at `-1` growing rightward (`++top1`), `top2` starts at `MAX` growing leftward (`--top2`). Overflow occurs only when `top1 + 1 == top2`, achieving optimal space sharing.
2. N Stacks in One Array: Divide array into $N$ equal segments of size `MAX / N` with boundary pointers `B[i]` and top pointers `T[i]`. If stack $i$ exceeds its segment, shift boundary pointers or reallocate dynamically.
3. Multiple Queues: Similarly divide array into $N$ segments with separate `front[i]` and `rear[i]` pointers.
keyPoints: Two stacks growing towards each other utilize 100% of memory before overflowing.
Overflow for 2 stacks occurs only when top1 + 1 == top2.
N stacks in one array divide memory into segments with boundary B[i] and top T[i].
Dynamic boundary shifting allows an overflowing stack to borrow space from an adjacent underutilized stack.
Conserves memory overhead compared to allocating separate fixed-size buffers.

examModelAnswers.question: Explain how two stacks can be implemented efficiently in a single one-dimensional array. Write C functions for push1, push2, pop1, and pop2.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Approach:
Start Stack 1 at index -1 growing rightward (++top1). Start Stack 2 at index MAX growing leftward (--top2).

2. Overflow Condition:
`top1 + 1 == top2`. Neither stack overflows until the entire array is filled.

3. Underflow Conditions:
`top1 == -1` for Stack 1; `top2 == MAX` for Stack 2.
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Award 2 marks for memory diagram, 3 marks for push/pop functions, 2 marks for boundary conditions.

vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t2.title: Multiple Stacks and Queues
vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: Multiple stacks in one array is like sharing a long double-ended train car: Stack 1 starts filling seats from the front moving backward, while Stack 2 starts filling seats from the back moving forward. They only collide when the entire train is completely full.
vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
Partitioning a single contiguous array `V[MAX]` to house multiple stacks or queues:
1. Two Stacks in One Array: `top1` starts at `-1` growing rightward (`++top1`), `top2` starts at `MAX` growing leftward (`--top2`). Overflow occurs only when `top1 + 1 == top2`, achieving optimal space sharing.
2. N Stacks in One Array: Divide array into $N$ equal segments of size `MAX / N` with boundary pointers `B[i]` and top pointers `T[i]`. If stack $i$ exceeds its segment, shift boundary pointers or reallocate dynamically.
3. Multiple Queues: Similarly divide array into $N$ segments with separate `front[i]` and `rear[i]` pointers.
keyPoints: Two stacks growing towards each other utilize 100% of memory before overflowing.
Overflow for 2 stacks occurs only when top1 + 1 == top2.
N stacks in one array divide memory into segments with boundary B[i] and top T[i].
Dynamic boundary shifting allows an overflowing stack to borrow space from an adjacent underutilized stack.
Conserves memory overhead compared to allocating separate fixed-size buffers.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t3.simpleConcept: A singly linked list is like a treasure hunt: each clue written on a piece of paper tells you the secret code (data) and gives you the exact address to the next clue hidden in another room (pointer). You don't need all clues stored in one box.
keyPoints: Nodes are dynamically allocated on the heap at runtime (no fixed size limits).
Non-contiguous memory allocation eliminates expensive array shifting during insertion/deletion.
Random access is NOT supported; accessing element k takes O(k) linear sequential traversal.
Extra memory overhead: each node stores an address pointer (4 or 8 bytes) alongside data.
Always check for NULL head and free memory after deletion to avoid memory leaks.

examModelAnswers.question: Define Singly Linked List. Write C functions to insert a node at the front and delete a node from the end of a singly linked list.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
A Singly Linked List is a linear data structure of nodes where each node contains a data field and a reference link pointer to the subsequent node.

2. Insert Front:
`newNode = malloc(); newNode->data = val; newNode->next = head; return newNode;`

3. Delete End:
If head == NULL return NULL. If head->next == NULL free(head), return NULL. Traverse with temp until temp->next->next == NULL. free(temp->next); temp->next = NULL; return head.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.title: Tree Terminology & Binary Trees Properties
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.simpleConcept: A tree data structure is like an inverted family pedigree or organizational chart: the CEO (root) sits at the very top, managers branch out below (internal nodes), and team members without direct reports are at the bottom (leaves).
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t1.technicalConcept:
A Tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of one root node and zero or more disjoint subtrees.
• Terminology:
  - Root: Unique top node with in-degree 0.
  - Degree of node: Number of subtrees/children attached to the node.
  - Leaf/Terminal node: Node with degree 0.
  - Level: Root is at level 0; children are at level + 1.
  - Height/Depth: Maximum level of any node in the tree.
• Binary Tree: Tree where every node has at most 2 children (left child and right child).
• Core Mathematical Properties:
  1. Maximum nodes at level $i$: $2^i$.
  2. Maximum nodes in binary tree of height $k$: $2^{k+1} - 1$.
  3. Leaf Node Formula: For any non-empty binary tree, $n_0 = n_2 + 1$ (leaves equals degree-2 nodes plus 1).
keyPoints: Trees represent hierarchical parent-child relationships.
Binary tree restricts each node to at most two children (left and right).
Maximum nodes at level i is 2^i (assuming root at level 0).
Maximum nodes in binary tree of depth k is 2^(k+1) - 1.
Fundamental relation: Number of leaf nodes n0 is always n2 + 1 (nodes of degree 2 plus 1).

examModelAnswers.question: Define the following tree terms: Root, Degree, Depth, Leaf, Path. Prove that for any non-empty binary tree with n nodes and e edges, e = n - 1.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Terminology Definitions:
• Root: Top node with no parent.
• Degree: Number of direct children of a node.
• Leaf: Node with degree 0.
• Depth: Length of path from root to node.
• Path: Sequence of consecutive edges connecting nodes.

2. Proof of e = n - 1:
Every node in a tree except the root has exactly one incoming edge from its parent. Since there are n nodes and only the root has no parent, the total number of incoming edges must be n - 1. Thus, e = n - 1.
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Award 5 marks for 5 definitions, 3 marks for mathematical proof.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.title: Array and Linked Representation of Binary Trees
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.simpleConcept: Storing a binary tree in an array is like assigning house numbers on a planned street: parent house i always has left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2. Linked representation is like freeform land where each house has two directional pointers pointing to neighbor lots.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t2.technicalConcept:
Two fundamental ways to represent binary trees in memory:
1. Sequential (Array) Representation:
• Store nodes in a 1D array `tree[MAX]` using level-order index mapping (0-based):
  - Left child of node `i`: `2 * i + 1`
  - Right child of node `i`: `2 * i + 2`
  - Parent of node `i`: `(i - 1) / 2`
• Pros: Direct random access without pointers.
• Cons: Wastes massive space ($O(2^h)$) for skewed binary trees.
2. Linked (Pointer) Representation:
• Each node has `data`, `left` pointer, and `right` pointer (`struct TreeNode*`).
• Pros: Efficient memory allocation scaling directly with $N$ nodes ($O(N)$ space).
• Cons: Extra pointer memory overhead.
keyPoints: Array representation maps node i to left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2.
Array representation is optimal for Complete Binary Trees (compact storage).
Array representation wastes significant space for sparse or skewed trees.
Linked representation uses left and right pointers per node, dynamically allocated.
Linked representation is the universal standard for non-complete trees.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.title: Graph ADT & Elementary Graph Operations
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.simpleConcept: A graph is like a city airline route map: airports are vertices (nodes) and direct flights are edges. Breadth-First Search spreads like a radar wave (layer-by-layer), while Depth-First Search explores one flight connection to the end of the line before backtracking.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t1.technicalConcept:
A Graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of vertices $V$ and edges $E$.
1. Representations:
• Adjacency Matrix: $V \times V$ 2D array where `adj[u][v] = 1` if edge $(u,v)$ exists ($O(V^2)$ space).
• Adjacency List: Array of $V$ linked lists where `list[u]` stores all neighbors of $u$ ($O(V + E)$ space, optimal for sparse graphs).
2. Elementary Operations:
• Breadth-First Search (BFS): Explores vertices level-by-level using an auxiliary FIFO Queue ($O(V + E)$).
• Depth-First Search (DFS): Explores as deep as possible along each branch using recursion / Stack ($O(V + E)$).
• Connected Components: Finding maximal connected subgraphs using DFS/BFS sweeps.
keyPoints: Adjacency Matrix uses O(V^2) space; ideal for dense graphs.
Adjacency List uses O(V + E) space; optimal for sparse graphs.
BFS uses a FIFO queue and finds shortest unweighted paths.
DFS uses a stack or recursion and is used for cycle detection and topological sorting.
Both BFS and DFS maintain a visited[] boolean array to avoid infinite loops in cyclic graphs.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.title: Hashing (Introduction & Static Hashing)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.simpleConcept: Hashing is like coat-check at a theater: instead of searching every coat on the rack (O(N)), the attendant hands you ticket number 42 derived directly from your token, so you walk straight to hook 42 in O(1) instant time.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t2.technicalConcept:
Hashing maps a large key space to a compact array index `0...m-1` (Hash Table) using a Hash Function $h(k)$.
1. Common Hash Functions:
• Division Method: $h(k) = k \pmod{m}$ ($m$ prime close to table size).
• Mid-Square Method: Square key $k^2$ and extract middle $r$ digits.
• Folding Method: Divide key into parts and sum them.
2. Collision Resolution Techniques (Open Addressing & Chaining):
• Collision: When $h(k_1) = h(k_2)$ for $k_1 \neq k_2$.
• Linear Probing: When collision occurs, probe consecutive slots `(h(k) + i) % m`. Suffers from Primary Clustering.
• Quadratic Probing: Probes `(h(k) + i^2) % m`. Reduces clustering.
• Separate Chaining: Each slot points to a linked list of collided keys ($O(1 + \alpha)$ average access where $\alpha = n/m$ is load factor).
keyPoints: Hash function maps large arbitrary keys to compact table index in O(1) time.
Collision occurs when two distinct keys hash to the same table index.
Linear Probing resolves collisions by checking next consecutive slot (suffers from clustering).
Quadratic Probing uses (h(k) + i^2) % m to eliminate primary clustering.
Separate Chaining stores collisions in an external linked list at each table bucket.

1BCS305_M2_T4.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion using Stack
1BCS305_M2_T4.simpleConcept: Converting Infix to Postfix is like a railway junction switchyard: numbers (operands) roll straight through to the output train. Operators must wait on a siding (the stack) until lower-priority trains arrive, which pushes the waiting higher-priority engines onto the track.
1BCS305_M2_T4.technicalConcept:
Shunting-Yard Infix to Postfix Conversion Algorithm:
1. Initialize operator stack with `#` (lowest precedence sentinel).
2. Scan tokens of infix string from left to right:
   • If operand: append directly to postfix output.
   • If `(`: push onto stack.
   • If `)`: pop and append to output until `(` is popped. Discard `(`.
   • If operator `op`: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (taking associativity into account), pop and append to output. Then push `op`.
3. At end of infix expression, pop all remaining operators onto postfix output.
• Time Complexity: $O(N)$ linear time where $N$ is expression length.
keyPoints: Operands pass directly to the output string without entering the stack.
Stack holds only operators and open parentheses.
An operator on stack pops when incoming operator has lesser or equal precedence.
Parentheses override precedence: '(' is pushed immediately, ')' flushes until '('.
Time complexity is O(N) as each token is pushed and popped at most once.

6. Token ')': pop '+' -> Output 'AB+'
7. Token '*': push '*'

9. Token '-': pop '*' -> Output 'AB+C*', push '-'

12. Token '-': push '-'
13. Token 'E': Output 'AB+C*DE'
14. Token ')': pop '-' -> Output 'AB+C*DE-'
15. End of outer parens: pop '-' -> Output 'AB+C*DE--'
16. Token '^': push '^'
17. Token '(': push '('
18. Token 'F': Output 'AB+C*DE--F'
19. Token '+': push '+'
20. Token 'G': Output 'AB+C*DE--FG'
21. Token ')': pop '+' -> Output 'AB+C*DE--FG+'
22. End of expression: pop '^' -> Final: `AB+C*DE--FG+^`.

1BCS305_M2_T5.title: Evaluation of Postfix Expression
1BCS305_M2_T5.simpleConcept: Evaluating a postfix expression is like calculating a grocery bill with an old HP reverse-Polish calculator: you type the numbers first (push 5, push 3), and when you hit '+', it takes both numbers, adds them, and leaves 8 ready for the next operation.
1BCS305_M2_T5.technicalConcept:
Postfix Evaluation Algorithm:
1. Initialize empty operand stack.
2. Scan postfix tokens from left to right:
   • If operand: convert to numeric value and push onto operand stack.
   • If operator `op`: pop operand `op2` (top), then pop operand `op1` (second top). Compute `res = op1 op op2`. Push `res` back onto stack.
3. At the end of expression, the final answer is the sole value remaining on the stack.
• Important Trap: Order matters for non-commutative operators: `op1 - op2` and `op1 / op2` (the first popped item is the RIGHT operand).
keyPoints: Stack holds operands and intermediate numeric results.
When operator arrives, pop two operands: op2 (first popped), op1 (second popped).
Operation is evaluated as (op1 operator op2), NOT (op2 operator op1).
Time complexity is strictly O(N) single forward scan.
After scanning all tokens, exactly one value remains on stack (the result).

examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Algorithm:
Scan token left to right. Push operands. When operator encountered, pop op2, pop op1. Compute op1 op op2. Push result. Final result is pop().

2. Trace:
• '6': push 6
• '2': push 2
• '3': push 3
• '+': pop 3, 2 -> 2+3=5, push 5 [Stack: 6, 5]
• '-': pop 5, 6 -> 6-5=1, push 1 [Stack: 1]
• '3': push 3 [Stack: 1, 3]
• '8': push 8 [Stack: 1, 3, 8]
• '2': push 2 [Stack: 1, 3, 8, 2]
• '/': pop 2, 8 -> 8/2=4, push 4 [Stack: 1, 3, 4]
• '+': pop 4, 3 -> 3+4=7, push 7 [Stack: 1, 7]
• '*': pop 7, 1 -> 1*7=7, push 7 [Stack: 7]
• '2': push 2 [Stack: 7, 2]
• '^': pop 2, 7 -> 7^2=49, push 49 [Stack: 49]
• '3': push 3 [Stack: 49, 3]
• '+': pop 3, 49 -> 49+3=52, push 52 [Stack: 52]
Final Answer: 52.

1BCS305_M2_T6.title: Queue Definition, Array Representation & Operations
1BCS305_M2_T6.simpleConcept: A queue is like a single-file ticket counter line: the first person to arrive is the first person served (FIFO: First-In, First-Out). New people join at the back (rear), and served people leave from the front.
1BCS305_M2_T6.technicalConcept:
A Queue is a linear list with FIFO (First-In First-Out) discipline where insertions occur exclusively at `rear` and deletions occur exclusively at `front`.
• Array Representation: Array `Q[MAX]` with integer indices `front = 0` and `rear = -1` (or `front = -1, rear = -1`).
• Enqueue (Insert): Increment `rear` and store `Q[++rear] = item`. Overflow when `rear == MAX - 1`.
• Dequeue (Delete): Return `item = Q[front++]`. Underflow when `front > rear` (or `front == -1`).
• Linear Queue Limitation (False Overflow): Once `rear` reaches `MAX - 1`, no new items can be inserted even if `front > 0` leaving empty slots at the beginning.
keyPoints: Queue enforces FIFO (First-In First-Out) discipline.
Insertions occur at rear; deletions occur at front.
Enqueue and Dequeue execute in O(1) constant time.
Linear array queue suffers from 'False Overflow' when rear reaches MAX - 1.
Used in OS CPU job scheduling, printer spoolers, and breadth-first search (BFS).

1BCS305_M3_T4.title: Linked Stacks and Queues
1BCS305_M3_T4.simpleConcept: A linked stack or queue is like adding and removing train cars using modular couplers on dynamic tracks: you never worry about parking lot boundaries because each new car is hitched on demand and unhitched when done.
1BCS305_M3_T4.technicalConcept:
Implementing Stacks and Queues using Singly Linked Lists eliminates static array overflow:
1. Linked Stack:
• Insertion (Push): Always performed at `head` of linked list: `newNode->next = top; top = newNode` ($O(1)$).
• Deletion (Pop): Always performed from `head`: `temp = top; top = top->next; free(temp)` ($O(1)$).
• Overflow: Occurs only if system heap memory is exhausted (`malloc() == NULL`).
2. Linked Queue:
• Maintained with two pointers: `front` (points to first node) and `rear` (points to last node).
• Enqueue: Add at `rear`: `rear->next = newNode; rear = newNode` ($O(1)$).
• Dequeue: Remove from `front`: `temp = front; front = front->next; free(temp)` ($O(1)$).
keyPoints: Linked Stack pushes and pops at the head node in O(1) constant time.
Linked Queue inserts at rear and deletes from front in O(1) constant time.
Eliminates static array overflow; grows dynamically as long as heap memory exists.
Underflow occurs when top == NULL (stack) or front == NULL (queue).
When the last queue node is dequeued, rear must also be reset to NULL.

1BCS305_M3_T5.title: Additional List Operations & Sparse Matrix using Linked List
1BCS305_M3_T5.simpleConcept: Connecting two linked lists is like coupling two trains together: you just point the last car of train A to the engine of train B. Representing a sparse matrix with linked lists is like storing only occupied seats with row/column tags, saving huge empty memory.

1BCS305_M4_T3.title: Binary Tree Traversals (Preorder, Inorder, Postorder)
1BCS305_M4_T3.simpleConcept: Walking around a tree is like visiting an art gallery with three recording styles: Preorder notes the artist's plaque before seeing paintings (V-L-R). Inorder views left wing, center sculpture, then right wing (L-V-R). Postorder inspects both wings before writing the summary (L-R-V).
1BCS305_M4_T3.technicalConcept:
Tree Traversal systematically visits every node in a binary tree exactly once.
1. Depth-First Traversals:
• Preorder Traversal ($V L R$):
  1. Visit current node ($V$)
  2. Traverse Left subtree ($L$)
  3. Traverse Right subtree ($R$)
• Inorder Traversal ($L V R$):
  1. Traverse Left subtree ($L$)
  2. Visit current node ($V$)
  3. Traverse Right subtree ($R$)
  (Note: Inorder of a BST outputs keys in strictly ascending sorted order).
• Postorder Traversal ($L R V$):
  1. Traverse Left subtree ($L$)
  2. Traverse Right subtree ($R$)
  3. Visit current node ($V$)
• Tree Reconstruction: A binary tree can be uniquely reconstructed given its Inorder traversal and either Preorder or Postorder traversal.
keyPoints: Preorder: Root -> Left -> Right (VLR).
Inorder: Left -> Root -> Right (LVR). Outputs sorted keys in BST.
Postorder: Left -> Right -> Root (LRV). Used for tree deletion and bottom-up evaluation.
Time complexity of all traversals is O(N) as each node is visited once.
Inorder combined with Preorder uniquely constructs a binary tree.

1BCS305_M4_T5.title: Binary Search Trees (Definition, Searching, Insertion)
1BCS305_M4_T5.simpleConcept: A Binary Search Tree is like an organized dictionary: for any word you look at, all words alphabetically earlier are kept on the left shelf, and all words alphabetically later are kept on the right shelf. This cuts your search time in half at every step.
1BCS305_M4_T5.technicalConcept:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree satisfying the BST ordering invariant:
• For any node $X$:
  - All keys in left subtree of $X$ are strictly less than $X.key$ (`left.key < X.key`).
  - All keys in right subtree of $X$ are strictly greater than $X.key$ (`right.key > X.key`).
  - Both left and right subtrees must themselves be BSTs.
• Searching Algorithm: Compare target $K$ with $root.key$. If equal, return found. If $K < root.key$, recurse left. If $K > root.key$, recurse right.
• Insertion Algorithm: Search for key; attach new node at the resulting NULL leaf position.
• Complexity: Search/Insert execute in $O(h)$ where $h$ is height ($O(\log N)$ for balanced tree, $O(N)$ for degenerate skewed tree).
keyPoints: BST property: left_subtree < root < right_subtree for every node.
Inorder traversal of any BST outputs keys in strictly increasing sorted order.
Search and insertion take O(h) time where h is the tree height.
In a balanced BST, h = O(log N). In a worst-case skewed tree, h = O(N).
Duplicate keys are typically disallowed or maintained with a frequency counter.

1BCS305_M4_T6.title: BST Deletion & Counting Binary Trees
1BCS305_M4_T6.simpleConcept: Deleting a node in a BST is like filling an executive vacancy: if the person has no subordinates, you just remove the desk (leaf). If they have one subordinate, that person gets promoted (1 child). If they have two branches, you promote the most senior person from the junior wing (inorder predecessor) or the most junior from the senior wing (inorder successor).
1BCS305_M4_T6.technicalConcept:
1. BST Deletion Algorithm (3 Cases):
• Case 1: Node to be deleted is a Leaf (0 children). Simply free node and set parent's pointer to `NULL`.
• Case 2: Node has One Child. Bypass node: connect parent directly to the single child and free node.
• Case 3: Node has Two Children. Find In-Order Successor (smallest node in right subtree) or In-Order Predecessor (largest in left subtree). Copy successor's key to current node, then recursively delete successor (which falls into Case 1 or 2).
2. Counting Structurally Unique Binary Trees:
• The number of structurally distinct binary trees with $N$ unlabeled nodes is given by the Catalan Number $C_N = \frac{1}{N+1} \binom{2N}{N}$.
• For $N$ distinct labeled keys, total unique BSTs is $C_N \times N!$.
keyPoints: Case 1 (Leaf): Free node directly and set parent link to NULL.
Case 2 (1 child): Bypass node by linking parent to child.
Case 3 (2 children): Replace with Inorder Successor (min of right subtree) or Inorder Predecessor.
Inorder successor is guaranteed to have at most one child.
Number of distinct binary trees with N nodes is Catalan number C(N) = (2N)! / ((N+1)! * N!).

1BCS305_M5_T3.title: Dynamic Hashing
1BCS305_M5_T3.simpleConcept: Static hashing is like a fixed-size apartment mailroom: when mailboxes overflow, you have no choice but to rebuild the entire room. Dynamic hashing uses modular folders (directories) that expand only the specific bucket that is overflowing without rebuilding everything.
1BCS305_M5_T3.technicalConcept:
Static hash tables degrade when key count $N$ grows significantly beyond capacity $M$, leading to long chains or full table failures. Dynamic Hashing (Extendible Hashing) adapts dynamically to table growth:
• Directory and Buckets: A central Directory of pointers of size $2^d$ (where $d$ is Global Depth), pointing to leaf Buckets of capacity $B$ with Local Depth $p$.
• Key Lookup: Uses the first $d$ bits of hash value $h(K)$ to index the directory.
• Bucket Split:
  - When a bucket overflows and $p < d$: Split bucket, distribute keys based on bit $p+1$, and increment local depth $p = p + 1$.
  - When a bucket overflows and $p == d$: Double the directory size ($d = d + 1$), creating two pointers per bucket, then split the bucket.
• Advantage: Trie-based dynamic growth; avoids re-hashing all keys.
keyPoints: Static hashing degrades as load factor grows; dynamic hashing grows smoothly on demand.
Extendible hashing uses a directory of pointers indexed by binary prefix bits.
Global depth (d) determines directory size: 2^d entries.
Local depth (p) determines number of bits shared by keys in a specific bucket.
Only the overflowing bucket splits; avoids global re-hashing of the entire database.

3. Bucket Split Procedure:

1BCS305_M5_T4.title: Priority Queues (Single & Double Ended)
1BCS305_M5_T4.simpleConcept: A regular queue serves whoever arrived first. A priority queue is like an emergency room triage: a patient with a severe condition gets treated ahead of patients with minor issues, regardless of arrival order.
1BCS305_M5_T4.technicalConcept:
A Priority Queue is an ADT where each element has an associated priority; items are dequeued based on priority rather than arrival sequence.
1. Single-Ended Priority Queue:
• Operations: `insert(x)`, `deleteMin()` (Min-PQ) or `deleteMax()` (Max-PQ).
• Implementations:
  - Unsorted Array/List: Insert $O(1)$, Delete-Min $O(N)$.
  - Sorted Array/List: Insert $O(N)$, Delete-Min $O(1)$.
  - Binary Heap: Insert $O(\log N)$, Delete-Min $O(\log N)$ (Optimal practical choice).
2. Double-Ended Priority Queue (DEPQ):
• Supports both `deleteMin()` AND `deleteMax()` simultaneously.
• Operations: `insert(x)`, `getMin()`, `getMax()`, `deleteMin()`, `deleteMax()`.
• Efficient structures: Dual Heaps, Interval Heaps, Min-Max Heaps ($O(\log N)$ for both min and max operations).
keyPoints: Priority Queue dequeues elements by priority rank rather than arrival order.
Min-Priority Queue removes smallest element; Max-Priority Queue removes largest.
Binary Heap provides balanced O(log N) insertion and deletion.
Double-Ended Priority Queue (DEPQ) supports BOTH deleteMin and deleteMax in O(log N).
Essential in Dijkstra shortest path, Prim MST, and task priority schedulers.

1BCS305_M5_T5.title: Leftist Trees
1BCS305_M5_T5.simpleConcept: A standard binary heap is stubborn to merge: merging two heaps takes O(N) rebuilding time. A Leftist Tree is intentionally designed lopsided (leaning left) so that merging two priority queues happens exclusively along their short right boundaries in O(log N) lightning speed.
1BCS305_M5_T5.technicalConcept:
A Leftist Tree is a binary tree priority queue designed for fast $O(\log N)$ merging.
• Shortest Path Length (s-value / Null Path Length):
  - $s(x)$ is the length of the shortest path from node $x$ to an external (NULL) node.
  - $s(\text{NULL}) = 0$.
  - $s(x) = 1 + \min(s(x.left), s(x.right))$.
• Leftist Property:
  - For every internal node $x$, $s(x.left) \ge s(x.right)$.
  - This forces the right subtree to always have the shortest path to an external node.
• Right Spine Theorem:
  - A leftist tree with $N$ nodes has a right spine length of at most $\lfloor \log_2(N + 1) \rfloor$.
• Merge Algorithm: Recursively merge right spines in $O(\log N)$ time; if leftist property is violated ($s(left) < s(right)$), swap left and right subtrees.
keyPoints: Leftist tree is a priority queue designed specifically for O(log N) merging.
s-value s(x) is the shortest distance from node x to an external NULL node.
Leftist property: s(left) >= s(right) for every node.
The right spine has the shortest path to a NULL node (at most log2(N+1) length).
Merging two leftist trees takes O(log N) by recursively merging along right spines.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t1.title: Classifications of Data Structures (Primitive & Non-Primitive)
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t1.simpleConcept: Think of data structures like kitchen containers. A single spice jar holds one item (primitive data types like int, float, char). A layered bento box or spice rack organizes multiple items together in a structured way (non-primitive data structures like arrays, stacks, and linked lists). Choosing the right container makes cooking (computing) fast and clean.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t1.technicalConcept:
Data structures are categorized into:
1. Primitive Data Structures: Basic types directly supported by hardware and machine instructions (int, float, char, pointer, double).
2. Non-Primitive Data Structures: Derived complex structures organizing collections of data elements.
   • Linear Data Structures: Elements form a sequential sequence (Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists). In linear structures, elements have unique predecessors and successors (except first and last).
   • Non-Linear Data Structures: Elements form hierarchical or interconnected relationships (Trees, Graphs). Each element may connect to multiple items.
keyPoints: Primitive types (int, char, float) operate directly via CPU registers and ALU instructions.
Non-primitive types organize multiple homogeneous or heterogeneous values.
Linear data structures maintain single-level sequential relationships (Arrays, Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues).
Non-linear structures represent hierarchical (Trees) or arbitrary network relationships (Graphs).
Primary operations include Insertion, Deletion, Traversal, Searching, Sorting, and Merging.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t2.title: Pointers & Dynamic Memory Allocation in C
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t2.simpleConcept: A pointer is a note with a house address instead of the house itself. Dynamic memory allocation is like booking a hotel room: you don't decide how many rooms you need when building the hotel (compile-time); you ask the front desk (OS) for exactly the rooms you need when guests arrive (runtime using malloc/calloc), and you must check out (free) when you leave so memory isn't wasted.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t2.technicalConcept:
Pointers store memory addresses of variables. The dereference operator `*` accesses the value at that address, while address-of `&` retrieves the memory address.
Dynamic Memory Allocation (DMA) allocates heap memory at runtime via standard library `<stdlib.h>` functions:
1. `malloc(size)`: Allocates `size` uninitialized bytes; returns `void*` or NULL on failure.
2. `calloc(n, size)`: Allocates contiguous block for `n` items of `size` bytes each and initializes all bits to 0.
3. `realloc(ptr, new_size)`: Resizes previously allocated heap block, preserving existing content.
4. `free(ptr)`: Deallocates heap block to prevent memory leaks.
keyPoints: Pointer declaration `type *ptr` holds an address in virtual memory.
malloc() leaves allocated memory uninitialized with garbage values.
calloc() clears memory to zero, useful for arrays and counters.
Always check `ptr != NULL` after heap allocations to avoid segmentation faults.
Failing to call `free()` leads to memory leaks; accessing after `free()` creates dangling pointer bugs.

• Performance: `malloc` is slightly faster as it skips zeroing memory.

2. Realloc and Free:

• `free(ptr)` returns memory back to heap pool.

3. Syntax and Check:

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t3.title: Arrays & Dynamic Allocation Arrays
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t3.simpleConcept: A static array is like a locked bookshelf with 5 fixed slots built into the wall. If you buy a 6th book, you are stuck. A dynamic array is a modular shelf on wheels: you can allocate 5 slots today, and if you need more space, you order a bigger shelf, move your books over, and discard the old one.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t3.technicalConcept:
Arrays are contiguous blocks of homogeneous data elements accessible via zero-based indexing.
• 1D Array Address Formula: `Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + (i - LowerBound) * ElementSize`
• 2D Row-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(i * ColCount) + j] * ElementSize`
• 2D Column-Major Formula: `Address(A[i][j]) = BaseAddress + [(j * RowCount) + i] * ElementSize`
Dynamic arrays overcome fixed compile-time dimensions by allocating heap pointers through `malloc/realloc`.
keyPoints: Arrays guarantee O(1) constant time random access by index.
Insertion and deletion in arbitrary positions require O(n) element shifting.
Row-major order stores elements row-by-row in linear memory (standard in C/C++).
Dynamic 2D arrays can be created via an array of pointers (`int **mat = malloc(rows * sizeof(int*))`).

examModelAnswers.question: Derive the address formula for a 2-dimensional array stored in Row-Major and Column-Major order.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
Let array A have bounds A[0...M-1][0...N-1], Base address = B, and element size = w bytes.

1. Row-Major Order:
• Elements are stored row-by-row.
• To reach element A[i][j], we must skip 'i' complete rows. Each row has 'N' elements, so `i * N` elements precede the current row.
• In row 'i', we must skip 'j' elements to reach column 'j'.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(i * N) + j] * w`.

2. Column-Major Order:
• Elements are stored column-by-column.
• Formula: `Loc(A[i][j]) = B + [(j * M) + i] * w`.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t4.technicalConcept:
• `struct`: Composite data type where every member has its own distinct memory offset. Total size >= sum of member sizes (plus padding).
• `union`: Members share the exact same starting memory address. Total size = size of its largest member.
• Polynomial Representation: A polynomial P(x) = a_n x^e + ... + a_0 is represented in memory as an array of structures or linked list where each node stores `coefficient` and `exponent`.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t5.title: Sparse Matrix Representation (Triplet Form)
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t5.simpleConcept: Imagine an attendance sheet with 1,000 students where only 3 students are absent. Instead of printing 1,000 names with 'Present' next to 997 of them, you just write down the 3 roll numbers who are absent. That is a sparse matrix: when most entries are zeros, we only store the non-zero values with their (row, column, value) coordinates.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t5.technicalConcept:
A sparse matrix is an M x N matrix in which the majority of elements are zero. Storing all elements in a standard 2D array wastes memory (O(M x N)) and CPU cycles processing zeroes.
Triplet Representation (3-Tuple Form):
An array of structures where each element has:
• `row`: Row index of non-zero value
• `col`: Column index of non-zero value
• `val`: Non-zero value
Row 0 (Header/Metadata) stores:
• `triplet[0].row = Total Rows (M)`
• `triplet[0].col = Total Columns (N)`
• `triplet[0].val = Total Non-Zero Elements (K)`
The total space occupied is (K + 1) * 3, dramatically smaller when K << M * N.
keyPoints: A matrix is sparse if zero elements significantly outnumber non-zero elements.
Standard 2D array uses O(rows * cols); Triplet form uses O(non_zeros) storage.
Row 0 is the metadata header storing matrix dimensions and total non-zero count.
Triplets are traditionally sorted by row index, then by column index.
