vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t6.title: Transposing a Sparse Matrix
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t6.simpleConcept: Transposing means turning rows into columns (swapping i and j coordinates). If you just swap coordinates naively, the resulting triplet list won't be sorted by rows anymore! An ordinary transpose searches through all columns one by one, which is slow. Fast Transpose uses a frequency count to precalculate the exact destination slot for every element in one smooth pass.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m1-t6.technicalConcept:
When transposing a sparse triplet representation, swapping `row` and `col` invalidates row-major ordering.
1. Ordinary Transpose: Iterates columns 0 to N-1; scans all K non-zero elements. Time: O(Cols * K).
2. Fast Transpose: Uses `row_terms[]` and `starting_pos[]` to place elements directly into target slots in a single pass. Time: O(Cols + K).
keyPoints: Transposing swaps (row, col) coordinates while preserving sorted row order.
Ordinary Transpose has O(cols * non_zeros) time complexity.
Fast Transpose achieves O(cols + non_zeros) using row_terms[] and starting_pos[] auxiliary arrays.
Fast Transpose requires O(cols) auxiliary memory space.

2. Auxiliary Arrays:

• `starting_pos[col]`: Prefix sum starting index in transposed matrix B: `starting_pos[i] = starting_pos[i-1] + row_terms[i-1]` with `starting_pos[0] = 1`.

3. Complexity Analysis:
• Loop 1: O(terms)
• Loop 2: O(cols)
• Loop 3: O(terms)
Total Time Complexity = O(cols + terms), which is linear.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t1.title: Stack Definition, Array Representation & Operations
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t1.simpleConcept: A stack is like a spring-loaded plate dispenser in a cafeteria: plates can only be added to or removed from the very top (LIFO: Last In, First Out). The last clean plate placed on top is the first one taken by the next customer.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t1.technicalConcept:
A Stack is a restricted linear data structure operating under the LIFO (Last-In First-Out) discipline where all insertions and deletions occur at a single end called `top`.
• Array Representation: An array `stack[MAX]` with integer pointer `top` initialized to `-1`.
• Push Operation: Check overflow (`top == MAX - 1`), increment `top`, and store `stack[++top] = item` (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
• Pop Operation: Check underflow (`top == -1`), retrieve `item = stack[top--]` (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
• Peek Operation: Inspect element at `top` without modifying pointer state (Time Complexity: $O(1)$).
keyPoints: Stack enforces strict LIFO (Last-In First-Out) access control.
Stack Overflow occurs when attempting push on full array (top == MAX - 1).
Stack Underflow occurs when attempting pop on empty array (top == -1).
All core operations (push, pop, peek, isEmpty, isFull) execute in O(1) constant time.
Common applications: Function call runtime stack, recursive backtracking, syntax parsing, and undo-redo buffers.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t2.title: Stacks using Dynamic Arrays
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t2.simpleConcept: A static stack is like a fixed-size egg carton with 6 slots; once full, you can't add more. A dynamic stack is like an accordion file that automatically doubles in size whenever you run out of slots, copying your files over smoothly.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t2.technicalConcept:
Fixed-size array stacks suffer from static memory limits. Dynamic array stacks allocate memory on the heap and automatically double capacity when full.
• Allocation: Initially allocate `capacity` elements via `malloc()`.
• Doubling Strategy: When `top == capacity - 1`, allocate `newCapacity = 2 * capacity` via `realloc()`.
• Amortized Complexity: While an occasional reallocation costs $O(N)$ copying time, the amortized cost per push over $N$ insertions remains $O(1)$.
• Memory Cleanup: Requires `free()` on stack destruction to prevent heap memory leaks.
keyPoints: Overcomes fixed compile-time stack limits using heap dynamic memory.
Uses realloc() to resize the contiguous memory block.
Doubling strategy achieves O(1) amortized push complexity.
Always verify realloc return pointer != NULL before overwriting existing pointer.
Must free the allocated buffer when stack lifecycle terminates.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t3.title: Polish Notation (Infix, Prefix, Postfix)
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t3.simpleConcept: When humans write math, we place operators between numbers (Infix: A + B). But computers find parentheses and operator precedence messy. Polish notation puts operators in front (Prefix: + A B) or after (Postfix: A B +), removing all need for parentheses.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m2-t3.technicalConcept:
Notations for arithmetic expressions:
1. Infix Notation: Operator is placed between operands: `A + B`. Requires operator precedence, associativity, and parentheses for unambiguous evaluation.
2. Prefix (Polish) Notation: Operator precedes operands: `+ A B`.
3. Postfix (Reverse Polish) Notation: Operator follows operands: `A B +`.
• Operator Precedence Hierarchy: Parentheses `()` > Exponentiation `^` ($R \to L$) > Multiplication/Division `*`, `/` ($L \to R$) > Addition/Subtraction `+`, `-` ($L \to R$).
• Advantages of Postfix: Eliminates parentheses, does not require look-ahead parsing, and evaluates linearly using a single stack pass.
keyPoints: Infix requires operator precedence, associativity, and parentheses rules.
Postfix and Prefix require NO parentheses and NO precedence parsing during evaluation.
Exponentiation (^) is Right-to-Left associative; +, -, *, / are Left-to-Right associative.

examModelAnswers.question: What is Polish notation? Differentiate between Infix, Prefix, and Postfix notations with examples.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
Polish notation (devised by Jan Łukasiewicz) is a notation format where operator placement determines evaluation order without parentheses.

2. Comparison:
• Infix: `<operand> <operator> <operand>` (e.g. `(A + B) * C`)
• Prefix: `<operator> <operand> <operand>` (e.g. `* + A B C`)
• Postfix: `<operand> <operand> <operator>` (e.g. `A B + C *`)

3. Advantages:
Postfix expressions can be evaluated directly in one forward scan using a stack.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t4.title: Infix to Postfix Conversion using Stack
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t4.simpleConcept: Converting Infix to Postfix is like a railway junction switchyard: numbers (operands) roll straight through to the output train. Operators must wait on a siding (the stack) until lower-priority trains arrive, which pushes the waiting higher-priority engines onto the track.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t4.technicalConcept:
Shunting-Yard Infix to Postfix Conversion Algorithm:
1. Initialize operator stack with `#` (lowest precedence sentinel).
2. Scan tokens of infix string from left to right:
   • If operand: append directly to postfix output.
   • If `(`: push onto stack.
   • If `)`: pop and append to output until `(` is popped. Discard `(`.
   • If operator `op`: while stack top has higher or equal precedence (taking associativity into account), pop and append to output. Then push `op`.
3. At end of infix expression, pop all remaining operators onto postfix output.
• Time Complexity: $O(N)$ linear time where $N$ is expression length.

Stack holds only operators and open parentheses.
An operator on stack pops when incoming operator has lesser or equal precedence.
Parentheses override precedence: '(' is pushed immediately, ')' flushes until '('.
Time complexity is O(N) as each token is pushed and popped at most once.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t5.title: Evaluation of Postfix Expression
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t5.simpleConcept: Evaluating a postfix expression is like calculating a grocery bill with an old HP reverse-Polish calculator: you type the numbers first (push 5, push 3), and when you hit '+', it takes both numbers, adds them, and leaves 8 ready for the next operation.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t5.technicalConcept:
Postfix Evaluation Algorithm:
1. Initialize empty operand stack.
2. Scan postfix tokens from left to right:
   • If operand: convert to numeric value and push onto operand stack.
   • If operator `op`: pop operand `op2` (top), then pop operand `op1` (second top). Compute `res = op1 op op2`. Push `res` back onto stack.
3. At the end of expression, the final answer is the sole value remaining on the stack.
• Important Trap: Order matters for non-commutative operators: `op1 - op2` and `op1 / op2` (the first popped item is the RIGHT operand).
keyPoints: Stack holds operands and intermediate numeric results.
When operator arrives, pop two operands: op2 (first popped), op1 (second popped).
Operation is evaluated as (op1 operator op2), NOT (op2 operator op1).
Time complexity is strictly O(N) single forward scan.
After scanning all tokens, exactly one value remains on stack (the result).

examModelAnswers.question: Write the algorithm to evaluate a postfix expression. Trace the evaluation of: 6 2 3 + - 3 8 2 / + * 2 ^ 3 +
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Algorithm:
Scan token left to right. Push operands. When operator encountered, pop op2, pop op1. Compute op1 op op2. Push result. Final result is pop().

2. Trace:
• '6': push 6
• '2': push 2
• '3': push 3
• '+': pop 3, 2 -> 2+3=5, push 5 [Stack: 6, 5]
• '-': pop 5, 6 -> 6-5=1, push 1 [Stack: 1]
• '3': push 3 [Stack: 1, 3]
• '8': push 8 [Stack: 1, 3, 8]
• '2': push 2 [Stack: 1, 3, 8, 2]
• '/': pop 2, 8 -> 8/2=4, push 4 [Stack: 1, 3, 4]
• '+': pop 4, 3 -> 3+4=7, push 7 [Stack: 1, 7]
• '*': pop 7, 1 -> 1*7=7, push 7 [Stack: 7]
• '2': push 2 [Stack: 7, 2]
• '^': pop 2, 7 -> 7^2=49, push 49 [Stack: 49]
• '3': push 3 [Stack: 49, 3]
• '+': pop 3, 49 -> 49+3=52, push 52 [Stack: 52]
Final Answer: 52.
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Award 3 marks for algorithm steps, 5 marks for trace table and correct final value (52).

   • If operand: convert to numeric value and push onto operand stack.
   • If operator `op`: pop operand `op2` (top), then pop operand `op1` (second top). Compute `res = op1 op op2`. Push `res` back onto stack.
3. At the end of expression, the final answer is the sole value remaining on the stack.
• Important Trap: Order matters for non-commutative operators: `op1 - op2` and `op1 / op2` (the first popped item is the RIGHT operand).
keyPoints: Stack holds operands and intermediate numeric results.
When operator arrives, pop two operands: op2 (first popped), op1 (second popped).
Operation is evaluated as (op1 operator op2), NOT (op2 operator op1).
Time complexity is strictly O(N) single forward scan.
After scanning all tokens, exactly one value remains on stack (the result).

1. Algorithm:
Scan token left to right. Push operands. When operator encountered, pop op2, pop op1. Compute op1 op op2. Push result. Final result is pop().

• '3': push 3

• '3': push 3 [Stack: 49, 3]
• '+': pop 3, 49 -> 49+3=52, push 52 [Stack: 52]

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t6.title: Queue Definition, Array Representation & Operations
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t6.simpleConcept: A queue is like a single-file ticket counter line: the first person to arrive is the first person served (FIFO: First-In, First-Out). New people join at the back (rear), and served people leave from the front.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m2-t6.technicalConcept:
A Queue is a linear list with FIFO (First-In First-Out) discipline where insertions occur exclusively at `rear` and deletions occur exclusively at `front`.
• Array Representation: Array `Q[MAX]` with integer indices `front = 0` and `rear = -1` (or `front = -1, rear = -1`).
• Enqueue (Insert): Increment `rear` and store `Q[++rear] = item`. Overflow when `rear == MAX - 1`.
• Dequeue (Delete): Return `item = Q[front++]`. Underflow when `front > rear` (or `front == -1`).
• Linear Queue Limitation (False Overflow): Once `rear` reaches `MAX - 1`, no new items can be inserted even if `front > 0` leaving empty slots at the beginning.
keyPoints: Queue enforces FIFO (First-In First-Out) discipline.
Insertions occur at rear; deletions occur at front.
Enqueue and Dequeue execute in O(1) constant time.
Linear array queue suffers from 'False Overflow' when rear reaches MAX - 1.
Used in OS CPU job scheduling, printer spoolers, and breadth-first search (BFS).

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t1.title: Circular Queues (Array & Dynamic)
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t1.simpleConcept: A circular queue is like a revolving sushi bar or carousel: when you reach the last seat at the end of the counter, the next seat wraps right back around to seat 0, ensuring no empty space is ever wasted.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t1.technicalConcept:
Circular Queues eliminate the false overflow of linear queues by conceptually connecting `MAX - 1` back to `0` using modulo arithmetic.
• Pointer Increment: `rear = (rear + 1) % MAX` and `front = (front + 1) % MAX`.
• Full Condition: `(rear + 1) % MAX == front` (reserves one sentinel slot to distinguish full from empty).
• Empty Condition: `front == rear`.
• Dynamic Circular Queue: When full, reallocates array with double capacity and unwraps the circular segments `[front...MAX-1]` and `[0...rear]` into a clean linear contiguous sequence `0...N-1`.
keyPoints: Uses modulo arithmetic (rear + 1) % MAX to wrap pointers around array boundaries.
Eliminates false overflow and achieves 100% space utilization.
Empty condition: front == rear. Full condition: (rear + 1) % MAX == front.
One array slot is reserved as a sentinel to distinguish full from empty states.
Dynamic circular queue requires linear unwrapping during realloc buffer expansion.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t2.title: Multiple Stacks and Queues
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t2.simpleConcept: Multiple stacks in one array is like sharing a long double-ended train car: Stack 1 starts filling seats from the front moving backward, while Stack 2 starts filling seats from the back moving forward. They only collide when the entire train is completely full.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t2.technicalConcept:
Partitioning a single contiguous array `V[MAX]` to house multiple stacks or queues:
1. Two Stacks in One Array: `top1` starts at `-1` growing rightward (`++top1`), `top2` starts at `MAX` growing leftward (`--top2`). Overflow occurs only when `top1 + 1 == top2`, achieving optimal space sharing.
2. N Stacks in One Array: Divide array into $N$ equal segments of size `MAX / N` with boundary pointers `B[i]` and top pointers `T[i]`. If stack $i$ exceeds its segment, shift boundary pointers or reallocate dynamically.
3. Multiple Queues: Similarly divide array into $N$ segments with separate `front[i]` and `rear[i]` pointers.
keyPoints: Two stacks growing towards each other utilize 100% of memory before overflowing.
Overflow for 2 stacks occurs only when top1 + 1 == top2.
N stacks in one array divide memory into segments with boundary B[i] and top T[i].
Dynamic boundary shifting allows an overflowing stack to borrow space from an adjacent underutilized stack.
Conserves memory overhead compared to allocating separate fixed-size buffers.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t4.title: Linked Stacks and Queues
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t4.simpleConcept: A linked stack or queue is like adding and removing train cars using modular couplers on dynamic tracks: you never worry about parking lot boundaries because each new car is hitched on demand and unhitched when done.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t4.technicalConcept:
Implementing Stacks and Queues using Singly Linked Lists eliminates static array overflow:
1. Linked Stack:
• Insertion (Push): Always performed at `head` of linked list: `newNode->next = top; top = newNode` ($O(1)$).
• Deletion (Pop): Always performed from `head`: `temp = top; top = top->next; free(temp)` ($O(1)$).
• Overflow: Occurs only if system heap memory is exhausted (`malloc() == NULL`).
2. Linked Queue:
• Maintained with two pointers: `front` (points to first node) and `rear` (points to last node).
• Enqueue: Add at `rear`: `rear->next = newNode; rear = newNode` ($O(1)$).
• Dequeue: Remove from `front`: `temp = front; front = front->next; free(temp)` ($O(1)$).
keyPoints: Linked Stack pushes and pops at the head node in O(1) constant time.
Linked Queue inserts at rear and deletes from front in O(1) constant time.
Eliminates static array overflow; grows dynamically as long as heap memory exists.
Underflow occurs when top == NULL (stack) or front == NULL (queue).
When the last queue node is dequeued, rear must also be reset to NULL.

vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t4.title: Linked Stacks and Queues
vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t4.simpleConcept: A linked stack or queue is like adding and removing train cars using modular couplers on dynamic tracks: you never worry about parking lot boundaries because each new car is hitched on demand and unhitched when done.
vtu-iot-s3-bcs304-2025-m3-t4.technicalConcept:
Implementing Stacks and Queues using Singly Linked Lists eliminates static array overflow:
1. Linked Stack:
• Insertion (Push): Always performed at `head` of linked list: `newNode->next = top; top = newNode` ($O(1)$).
• Deletion (Pop): Always performed from `head`: `temp = top; top = top->next; free(temp)` ($O(1)$).
• Overflow: Occurs only if system heap memory is exhausted (`malloc() == NULL`).
2. Linked Queue:
• Maintained with two pointers: `front` (points to first node) and `rear` (points to last node).
• Enqueue: Add at `rear`: `rear->next = newNode; rear = newNode` ($O(1)$).
• Dequeue: Remove from `front`: `temp = front; front = front->next; free(temp)` ($O(1)$).
keyPoints: Linked Stack pushes and pops at the head node in O(1) constant time.
Linked Queue inserts at rear and deletes from front in O(1) constant time.
Eliminates static array overflow; grows dynamically as long as heap memory exists.
Underflow occurs when top == NULL (stack) or front == NULL (queue).
When the last queue node is dequeued, rear must also be reset to NULL.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t5.title: Additional List Operations & Sparse Matrix using Linked List
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t5.simpleConcept: Connecting two linked lists is like coupling two trains together: you just point the last car of train A to the engine of train B. Representing a sparse matrix with linked lists is like storing only occupied seats with row/column tags, saving huge empty memory.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m3-t5.technicalConcept:
1. Additional SLL Operations:
• Inversion (Reversal): Reverse links in a single pass using 3 pointers: `prev = NULL`, `curr = head`, `next = NULL`. In loop: `next = curr->next; curr->next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next`. Returns `prev` ($O(N)$ time, $O(1)$ space).
• Concatenation: Traverse list A to tail; set `tailA->next = headB` ($O(N_A)$).
2. Sparse Matrix Representation using Linked Lists:
• Orthogonal Header Node Scheme: Uses circular lists with header nodes for each row and each column.
• Node Fields: `row`, `col`, `value`, `right` (next node in row), `down` (next node in column).
• Advantage: Completely dynamic; efficient for sparse matrix addition and multiplication without shifting.
keyPoints: Inverting a linked list in-place requires 3 pointers (prev, curr, next) in O(N) time and O(1) space.
Concatenation links the tail of first list to the head of second list.
Sparse matrix linked representation uses orthogonal row and column circular chains.
Each matrix node stores row, col, value, right-pointer, and down-pointer.
Saves memory over 2D array representation when matrix sparsity is very high.

examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Invert Algorithm:
Use 3 pointers: prev, curr, next. Initialize prev = NULL, curr = head. Iterate while curr != NULL: save next = curr->next, reverse pointer curr->next = prev, advance prev = curr, curr = next. Return prev.

2. Sparse Matrix Linked Representation:
Use header nodes for each row and column. Nodes contain (row, col, value, right, down). Right pointer connects row elements; down pointer connects column elements.

examModelAnswers.question: What is a doubly linked list? Write C functions to insert a node to the left of a given node and delete a specific node in a doubly linked list.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Definition:
A Doubly Linked List is a two-way linked list where every node has pointers to both its predecessor (prev) and successor (next).

2. Insert Left:
Allocate newNode. newNode->prev = target->prev; newNode->next = target; if (target->prev != NULL) target->prev->next = newNode; target->prev = newNode.

3. Delete Node:
Bypass del: del->prev->next = del->next; del->next->prev = del->prev; free(del).
examModelAnswers.markingTip: Award 2 marks for node diagram, 3 marks for insert left function, 3 marks for delete function.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m4-t1.simpleConcept: A tree data structure is like an inverted family pedigree or organizational chart: the CEO (root) sits at the very top, managers branch out below (internal nodes), and team members without direct reports are at the bottom (leaves).
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m4-t1.technicalConcept:
A Tree is a non-linear hierarchical data structure consisting of one root node and zero or more disjoint subtrees.
• Terminology:
  - Root: Unique top node with in-degree 0.
  - Degree of node: Number of subtrees/children attached to the node.
  - Leaf/Terminal node: Node with degree 0.
  - Level: Root is at level 0; children are at level + 1.
  - Height/Depth: Maximum level of any node in the tree.
• Binary Tree: Tree where every node has at most 2 children (left child and right child).
• Core Mathematical Properties:
  1. Maximum nodes at level $i$: $2^i$.
  2. Maximum nodes in binary tree of height $k$: $2^{k+1} - 1$.
  3. Leaf Node Formula: For any non-empty binary tree, $n_0 = n_2 + 1$ (leaves equals degree-2 nodes plus 1).
keyPoints: Trees represent hierarchical parent-child relationships.
Binary tree restricts each node to at most two children (left and right).
Maximum nodes at level i is 2^i (assuming root at level 0).
Maximum nodes in binary tree of depth k is 2^(k+1) - 1.
Fundamental relation: Number of leaf nodes n0 is always n2 + 1 (nodes of degree 2 plus 1).

examModelAnswers.question: Define the following tree terms: Root, Degree, Depth, Leaf, Path. Prove that for any non-empty binary tree with n nodes and e edges, e = n - 1.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Terminology Definitions:
• Root: Top node with no parent.
• Degree: Number of direct children of a node.
• Leaf: Node with degree 0.
• Depth: Length of path from root to node.
• Path: Sequence of consecutive edges connecting nodes.

2. Proof of e = n - 1:
Every node in a tree except the root has exactly one incoming edge from its parent. Since there are n nodes and only the root has no parent, the total number of incoming edges must be n - 1. Thus, e = n - 1.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m4-t2.title: Array and Linked Representation of Binary Trees
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m4-t2.simpleConcept: Storing a binary tree in an array is like assigning house numbers on a planned street: parent house i always has left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2. Linked representation is like freeform land where each house has two directional pointers pointing to neighbor lots.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m4-t2.technicalConcept:
Two fundamental ways to represent binary trees in memory:
1. Sequential (Array) Representation:
• Store nodes in a 1D array `tree[MAX]` using level-order index mapping (0-based):
  - Left child of node `i`: `2 * i + 1`
  - Right child of node `i`: `2 * i + 2`
  - Parent of node `i`: `(i - 1) / 2`
• Pros: Direct random access without pointers.
• Cons: Wastes massive space ($O(2^h)$) for skewed binary trees.
2. Linked (Pointer) Representation:
• Each node has `data`, `left` pointer, and `right` pointer (`struct TreeNode*`).
• Pros: Efficient memory allocation scaling directly with $N$ nodes ($O(N)$ space).
• Cons: Extra pointer memory overhead.
keyPoints: Array representation maps node i to left child at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2.
Array representation is optimal for Complete Binary Trees (compact storage).
Array representation wastes significant space for sparse or skewed trees.
Linked representation uses left and right pointers per node, dynamically allocated.
Linked representation is the universal standard for non-complete trees.

2. Linked Representation:
Store using struct { data, *left, *right }. Dynamic allocation. No wasted slots. Disadvantage: pointer storage overhead.

3. Comparison Table:

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t3.title: Binary Tree Traversals (Preorder, Inorder, Postorder)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t3.simpleConcept: Walking around a tree is like visiting an art gallery with three recording styles: Preorder notes the artist's plaque before seeing paintings (V-L-R). Inorder views left wing, center sculpture, then right wing (L-V-R). Postorder inspects both wings before writing the summary (L-R-V).
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t3.technicalConcept:
Tree Traversal systematically visits every node in a binary tree exactly once.
1. Depth-First Traversals:
• Preorder Traversal ($V L R$):
  1. Visit current node ($V$)
  2. Traverse Left subtree ($L$)
  3. Traverse Right subtree ($R$)
• Inorder Traversal ($L V R$):
  1. Traverse Left subtree ($L$)
  2. Visit current node ($V$)
  3. Traverse Right subtree ($R$)
  (Note: Inorder of a BST outputs keys in strictly ascending sorted order).
• Postorder Traversal ($L R V$):
  1. Traverse Left subtree ($L$)
  2. Traverse Right subtree ($R$)
  3. Visit current node ($V$)
• Tree Reconstruction: A binary tree can be uniquely reconstructed given its Inorder traversal and either Preorder or Postorder traversal.
keyPoints: Preorder: Root -> Left -> Right (VLR).
Inorder: Left -> Root -> Right (LVR). Outputs sorted keys in BST.
Postorder: Left -> Right -> Root (LRV). Used for tree deletion and bottom-up evaluation.
Time complexity of all traversals is O(N) as each node is visited once.
Inorder combined with Preorder uniquely constructs a binary tree.

2. Tree Reconstruction:

• For Right Subtree (F, C): Preorder has 'C' first -> C is right child of A. Inorder has F before C -> F is left child of C.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t4.simpleConcept: In a standard binary tree, over half of all branch pointers are empty NULLs. A Threaded Binary Tree connects these unused dead-ends as guide ropes (threads) pointing directly to the next node in line, allowing you to walk the entire tree without a backpack (stack).
keyPoints: Repurposes N + 1 empty NULL pointers into in-order predecessor and successor threads.

Insertion and deletion are more complex due to thread maintenance.

examModelAnswers.question: What is a threaded binary tree? Explain the node structure and in-order traversal of a right-threaded binary tree with an example.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Concept:
In a binary tree of N nodes, N+1 link pointers are NULL. A Threaded Binary Tree replaces NULL pointers with threads pointing to in-order predecessor and successor nodes.

2. Node Structure:
struct TNode with data, left, right, and boolean flags lthread, rthread.

3. Traversal Mechanism:
Find leftmost node. Print node. If rthread == 1, follow thread directly. Else move right and find leftmost child in right subtree. Eliminates stack and recursion.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t5.title: Binary Search Trees (Definition, Searching, Insertion)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t5.simpleConcept: A Binary Search Tree is like an organized dictionary: for any word you look at, all words alphabetically earlier are kept on the left shelf, and all words alphabetically later are kept on the right shelf. This cuts your search time in half at every step.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t5.technicalConcept:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree satisfying the BST ordering invariant:
• For any node $X$:
  - All keys in left subtree of $X$ are strictly less than $X.key$ (`left.key < X.key`).
  - All keys in right subtree of $X$ are strictly greater than $X.key$ (`right.key > X.key`).
  - Both left and right subtrees must themselves be BSTs.
• Searching Algorithm: Compare target $K$ with $root.key$. If equal, return found. If $K < root.key$, recurse left. If $K > root.key$, recurse right.
• Insertion Algorithm: Search for key; attach new node at the resulting NULL leaf position.
• Complexity: Search/Insert execute in $O(h)$ where $h$ is height ($O(\log N)$ for balanced tree, $O(N)$ for degenerate skewed tree).
keyPoints: BST property: left_subtree < root < right_subtree for every node.
Inorder traversal of any BST outputs keys in strictly increasing sorted order.
Search and insertion take O(h) time where h is the tree height.
In a balanced BST, h = O(log N). In a worst-case skewed tree, h = O(N).
Duplicate keys are typically disallowed or maintained with a frequency counter.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t6.title: BST Deletion & Counting Binary Trees
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t6.simpleConcept: Deleting a node in a BST is like filling an executive vacancy: if the person has no subordinates, you just remove the desk (leaf). If they have one subordinate, that person gets promoted (1 child). If they have two branches, you promote the most senior person from the junior wing (inorder predecessor) or the most junior from the senior wing (inorder successor).
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m4-t6.technicalConcept:
1. BST Deletion Algorithm (3 Cases):
• Case 1: Node to be deleted is a Leaf (0 children). Simply free node and set parent's pointer to `NULL`.
• Case 2: Node has One Child. Bypass node: connect parent directly to the single child and free node.
• Case 3: Node has Two Children. Find In-Order Successor (smallest node in right subtree) or In-Order Predecessor (largest in left subtree). Copy successor's key to current node, then recursively delete successor (which falls into Case 1 or 2).
2. Counting Structurally Unique Binary Trees:
• The number of structurally distinct binary trees with $N$ unlabeled nodes is given by the Catalan Number $C_N = \frac{1}{N+1} \binom{2N}{N}$.
• For $N$ distinct labeled keys, total unique BSTs is $C_N \times N!$.
keyPoints: Case 1 (Leaf): Free node directly and set parent link to NULL.
Case 2 (1 child): Bypass node by linking parent to child.
Case 3 (2 children): Replace with Inorder Successor (min of right subtree) or Inorder Predecessor.
Inorder successor is guaranteed to have at most one child.
Number of distinct binary trees with N nodes is Catalan number C(N) = (2N)! / ((N+1)! * N!).

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t1.title: Graph ADT & Elementary Graph Operations
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t1.simpleConcept: A graph is like a city airline route map: airports are vertices (nodes) and direct flights are edges. Breadth-First Search spreads like a radar wave (layer-by-layer), while Depth-First Search explores one flight connection to the end of the line before backtracking.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t1.technicalConcept:
A Graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of vertices $V$ and edges $E$.
1. Representations:
• Adjacency Matrix: $V \times V$ 2D array where `adj[u][v] = 1` if edge $(u,v)$ exists ($O(V^2)$ space).
• Adjacency List: Array of $V$ linked lists where `list[u]` stores all neighbors of $u$ ($O(V + E)$ space, optimal for sparse graphs).
2. Elementary Operations:

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t2.title: Hashing (Introduction & Static Hashing)
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t2.simpleConcept: Hashing is like coat-check at a theater: instead of searching every coat on the rack (O(N)), the attendant hands you ticket number 42 derived directly from your token, so you walk straight to hook 42 in O(1) instant time.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t2.technicalConcept:
Hashing maps a large key space to a compact array index `0...m-1` (Hash Table) using a Hash Function $h(k)$.
1. Common Hash Functions:
• Division Method: $h(k) = k \pmod{m}$ ($m$ prime close to table size).
• Mid-Square Method: Square key $k^2$ and extract middle $r$ digits.
• Folding Method: Divide key into parts and sum them.
2. Collision Resolution Techniques (Open Addressing & Chaining):
• Collision: When $h(k_1) = h(k_2)$ for $k_1 \neq k_2$.
• Linear Probing: When collision occurs, probe consecutive slots `(h(k) + i) % m`. Suffers from Primary Clustering.
• Quadratic Probing: Probes `(h(k) + i^2) % m`. Reduces clustering.
• Separate Chaining: Each slot points to a linked list of collided keys ($O(1 + \alpha)$ average access where $\alpha = n/m$ is load factor).
keyPoints: Hash function maps large arbitrary keys to compact table index in O(1) time.
Collision occurs when two distinct keys hash to the same table index.
Linear Probing resolves collisions by checking next consecutive slot (suffers from clustering).
Quadratic Probing uses (h(k) + i^2) % m to eliminate primary clustering.
Separate Chaining stores collisions in an external linked list at each table bucket.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t3.title: Dynamic Hashing
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t3.simpleConcept: Static hashing is like a fixed-size apartment mailroom: when mailboxes overflow, you have no choice but to rebuild the entire room. Dynamic hashing uses modular folders (directories) that expand only the specific bucket that is overflowing without rebuilding everything.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t3.technicalConcept:
Static hash tables degrade when key count $N$ grows significantly beyond capacity $M$, leading to long chains or full table failures. Dynamic Hashing (Extendible Hashing) adapts dynamically to table growth:
• Directory and Buckets: A central Directory of pointers of size $2^d$ (where $d$ is Global Depth), pointing to leaf Buckets of capacity $B$ with Local Depth $p$.
• Key Lookup: Uses the first $d$ bits of hash value $h(K)$ to index the directory.
• Bucket Split:
  - When a bucket overflows and $p < d$: Split bucket, distribute keys based on bit $p+1$, and increment local depth $p = p + 1$.
  - When a bucket overflows and $p == d$: Double the directory size ($d = d + 1$), creating two pointers per bucket, then split the bucket.
• Advantage: Trie-based dynamic growth; avoids re-hashing all keys.
keyPoints: Static hashing degrades as load factor grows; dynamic hashing grows smoothly on demand.
Extendible hashing uses a directory of pointers indexed by binary prefix bits.
Global depth (d) determines directory size: 2^d entries.
Local depth (p) determines number of bits shared by keys in a specific bucket.
Only the overflowing bucket splits; avoids global re-hashing of the entire database.

examModelAnswers.question: What is dynamic hashing? Explain extendible hashing with global depth, local depth, and bucket splitting mechanism.
examModelAnswers.stepByStepAnswer:
1. Need for Dynamic Hashing:
Static hash tables degrade as data volume fluctuates, requiring expensive full re-hashing. Dynamic hashing expands and contracts on demand.

2. Extendible Hashing Architecture:
• Directory: array of pointers indexed by d global depth bits (2^d size).
• Buckets: data pages holding up to B records with local depth p.

3. Bucket Split Procedure:
When bucket overflows: if p == d, double directory (d++). Increment p of overflowing bucket, allocate new bucket, and redistribute keys based on (p+1)-th bit.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t4.title: Priority Queues (Single & Double Ended)
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t4.simpleConcept: A regular queue serves whoever arrived first. A priority queue is like an emergency room triage: a patient with a severe condition gets treated ahead of patients with minor issues, regardless of arrival order.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t4.technicalConcept:
A Priority Queue is an ADT where each element has an associated priority; items are dequeued based on priority rather than arrival sequence.
1. Single-Ended Priority Queue:
• Operations: `insert(x)`, `deleteMin()` (Min-PQ) or `deleteMax()` (Max-PQ).
• Implementations:
  - Unsorted Array/List: Insert $O(1)$, Delete-Min $O(N)$.
  - Sorted Array/List: Insert $O(N)$, Delete-Min $O(1)$.
  - Binary Heap: Insert $O(\log N)$, Delete-Min $O(\log N)$ (Optimal practical choice).
2. Double-Ended Priority Queue (DEPQ):
• Supports both `deleteMin()` AND `deleteMax()` simultaneously.
• Operations: `insert(x)`, `getMin()`, `getMax()`, `deleteMin()`, `deleteMax()`.
• Efficient structures: Dual Heaps, Interval Heaps, Min-Max Heaps ($O(\log N)$ for both min and max operations).
keyPoints: Priority Queue dequeues elements by priority rank rather than arrival order.
Min-Priority Queue removes smallest element; Max-Priority Queue removes largest.
Binary Heap provides balanced O(log N) insertion and deletion.
Double-Ended Priority Queue (DEPQ) supports BOTH deleteMin and deleteMax in O(log N).
Essential in Dijkstra shortest path, Prim MST, and task priority schedulers.

A Priority Queue is an ADT where each element has a priority, and deletion retrieves the element with highest/lowest priority.

vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t4.simpleConcept: A regular queue serves whoever arrived first. A priority queue is like an emergency room triage: a patient with a severe condition gets treated ahead of patients with minor issues, regardless of arrival order.
vtu-aiml-s3-bcs304-2025-m5-t4.technicalConcept:
A Priority Queue is an ADT where each element has an associated priority; items are dequeued based on priority rather than arrival sequence.
1. Single-Ended Priority Queue:
• Operations: `insert(x)`, `deleteMin()` (Min-PQ) or `deleteMax()` (Max-PQ).
• Implementations:
  - Unsorted Array/List: Insert $O(1)$, Delete-Min $O(N)$.
  - Sorted Array/List: Insert $O(N)$, Delete-Min $O(1)$.
  - Binary Heap: Insert $O(\log N)$, Delete-Min $O(\log N)$ (Optimal practical choice).
2. Double-Ended Priority Queue (DEPQ):
• Supports both `deleteMin()` AND `deleteMax()` simultaneously.
• Operations: `insert(x)`, `getMin()`, `getMax()`, `deleteMin()`, `deleteMax()`.
• Efficient structures: Dual Heaps, Interval Heaps, Min-Max Heaps ($O(\log N)$ for both min and max operations).
keyPoints: Priority Queue dequeues elements by priority rank rather than arrival order.
Min-Priority Queue removes smallest element; Max-Priority Queue removes largest.
Binary Heap provides balanced O(log N) insertion and deletion.
Double-Ended Priority Queue (DEPQ) supports BOTH deleteMin and deleteMax in O(log N).
Essential in Dijkstra shortest path, Prim MST, and task priority schedulers.

vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t5.title: Leftist Trees
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t5.simpleConcept: A standard binary heap is stubborn to merge: merging two heaps takes O(N) rebuilding time. A Leftist Tree is intentionally designed lopsided (leaning left) so that merging two priority queues happens exclusively along their short right boundaries in O(log N) lightning speed.
vtu-cse-s3-1bcs305-2025-m5-t5.technicalConcept:
A Leftist Tree is a binary tree priority queue designed for fast $O(\log N)$ merging.
• Shortest Path Length (s-value / Null Path Length):
  - $s(x)$ is the length of the shortest path from node $x$ to an external (NULL) node.
  - $s(\text{NULL}) = 0$.
  - $s(x) = 1 + \min(s(x.left), s(x.right))$.
• Leftist Property:
  - For every internal node $x$, $s(x.left) \ge s(x.right)$.
  - This forces the right subtree to always have the shortest path to an external node.
• Right Spine Theorem:
  - A leftist tree with $N$ nodes has a right spine length of at most $\lfloor \log_2(N + 1) \rfloor$.
• Merge Algorithm: Recursively merge right spines in $O(\log N)$ time; if leftist property is violated ($s(left) < s(right)$), swap left and right subtrees.
keyPoints: Leftist tree is a priority queue designed specifically for O(log N) merging.
s-value s(x) is the shortest distance from node x to an external NULL node.
Leftist property: s(left) >= s(right) for every node.
The right spine has the shortest path to a NULL node (at most log2(N+1) length).
Merging two leftist trees takes O(log N) by recursively merging along right spines.
